Is it a fair assessment to say the project failed?
Teachers try to make a fair assessment of each student's work.

meaning: A careful examination that evaluates strengths and weaknesses rather than just describing.
usage: Verbs: write/provide/offer a critical analysis of something. “Critical” here means evaluative, not negative.
examples: Write a critical analysis of the article's main argument.
The book offers a critical analysis of modern capitalism.
A critical analysis requires more than summary.
Her essay was praised for its critical analysis.

meaning: An opinion that fairly considers all sides of an issue.
usage: Verbs: take/present/give/offer a balanced view. Also: a balanced argument/approach/account.
examples: A good essay presents a balanced view of the issue.
Try to take a balanced view before deciding.
The documentary offers a balanced view of the conflict.
Newspapers don't always give a balanced view.

meaning: An opinion based on facts rather than personal feelings.
usage: Verbs: take/form/get an objective view. Opposite: a subjective view.
examples: It's hard to take an objective view of your own work.
We need an objective view from an outside expert.
Researchers must try to maintain an objective view.
Ask a friend for an objective view of the situation.

meaning: Attention on a small, limited area of a subject.
usage: It can be positive (precise) or negative (too limited). Opposite: a broad focus. Verb: narrow the focus of something.
examples: The study has a narrow focus on one city.
A narrow focus can make your essay more manageable.
Critics say the course has too narrow a focus.
Start-ups often succeed by keeping a narrow focus.

meaning: A general description of the main features of a subject without details.
usage: Verbs: give/provide a broad overview of something. Similar: a general overview.
examples: The first lecture gives a broad overview of the course.
This chapter provides a broad overview of the topic.
Let me start with a broad overview before going into detail.
The report offers a broad overview of global trends.

meaning: To disagree strongly with someone or something.
usage: Pattern: take issue with someone/something (a claim/a point/someone's view). It is formal.
examples: I take issue with the claim that all students are lazy.
Several critics took issue with the author's conclusions.
She took issue with the way the data was presented.
I don't take issue with the goal, only the method.

meaning: To gradually accept a difficult or painful situation.
usage: Typical objects: a loss, a death, an illness, a defeat, the past. Irregular: came.
examples: She is still trying to come to terms with her father's death.
The country is coming to terms with its colonial past.
It took him months to come to terms with the diagnosis.
Fans have yet to come to terms with the defeat.

meaning: To move or develop at the same speed as someone or something.
usage: Typical objects: change, demand, technology, inflation, competitors. Also: keep up with.
examples: Wages have not kept pace with inflation.
Schools struggle to keep pace with technological change.
Supply can't keep pace with demand.
She worked hard to keep pace with the rest of the class.

meaning: To cause something to happen or exist.
usage: It is formal and often used for problems or ideas: give rise to concerns/speculation/new industries. Irregular: gave, given.
examples: The decision gave rise to widespread protests.
Industrialization gave rise to modern cities.
Poor diet can give rise to health problems.
His comments have given rise to speculation about his future.

meaning: To cause something to happen as a result.
usage: Pattern: lead to something/someone doing something. Irregular: led. Very common for cause and effect; “can/may lead to” for possible effects.
examples: Lack of sleep can lead to health problems.
The discovery led to a new treatment.
Poor communication led to misunderstandings.
Higher taxes may lead to lower spending.

meaning: To cause a particular situation or effect.
usage: Compare: A results in B (cause → effect) vs. B results from A (effect ← cause). Useful for varying cause-and-effect language.
examples: The accident resulted in two deaths.
Cutting staff could result in poorer service.
The policy resulted in higher unemployment.
Regular practice results in steady improvement.

meaning: To be caused by or develop from something.
usage: Pattern: problems/fears/ideas stem from something. It is not usually used in continuous or passive forms.
examples: Many health problems stem from poor diet.
Her interest in science stems from her childhood.
The conflict stems from a long history of mistrust.
Most of his anxiety stems from work.

meaning: To be one of the causes of something; also, to give help or money towards something.
usage: Pattern: contribute to something/doing something. Adverbs: contribute significantly/greatly to. Note “to” + -ing: “contributed to reducing costs”.
examples: Air pollution contributes to heart disease.
Many factors contributed to the company's success.
Everyone contributed to the discussion.
Tourism contributes significantly to the economy.

meaning: To have possible effects or consequences for someone or something.
usage: Adjectives: important/serious/far-reaching/major implications. Common in discussions of research findings.
examples: These findings have important implications for teachers.
The decision will have serious implications for the economy.
Climate change has implications for food security.
The new law has implications for every business.

meaning: To reduce or remove the difference between two things or groups.
usage: Pattern: bridge the gap between A and B. Similar: close/narrow the gap. Opposite: widen the gap.
examples: The programme aims to bridge the gap between school and work.
We need to bridge the gap between theory and practice.
Translation apps help bridge the language gap.
The charity works to bridge the gap between rich and poor.

meaning: To reduce the difference between two things.
usage: Pattern: narrow the gap between A and B. Also: close the gap; the gap narrows.
examples: The policy aims to narrow the gap between rich and poor.
The second-placed team has narrowed the gap to two points.
Investment in schools can narrow the gap in achievement.
The gender pay gap has narrowed slightly.

meaning: To increase the difference between two things.
usage: Pattern: widen the gap between A and B. Also: the gap widens. Often used of inequality.
examples: Critics say the tax cuts will widen the gap between rich and poor.
Technology may widen the gap between generations.
Online learning widened the gap between wealthy and poor students.
The gap in income has widened in recent decades.

meaning: To find a fair or sensible middle point between two opposing things.
usage: Pattern: strike a balance between A and B; strike the right balance. Irregular: struck.
examples: It's hard to strike a balance between work and family life.
The law tries to strike a balance between privacy and security.
Teachers must strike the right balance between support and challenge.
We struck a balance between cost and quality.

meaning: A very small difference between two things, often between something acceptable and something not.
usage: Pattern: There's a fine line between A and B; walk/tread a fine line.
examples: There's a fine line between confidence and arrogance.
Comedians walk a fine line between funny and offensive.
There's a fine line between persistence and stubbornness.
Journalists tread a fine line when reporting on private lives.

meaning: When something is not present or does not exist.
usage: Formal. Common objects: evidence, data, a cure, clear rules, a leader.
examples: In the absence of evidence, we cannot draw conclusions.
In the absence of a cure, prevention is essential.
The deputy manager will lead the meeting in the absence of the director.
In the absence of clear rules, people make their own.

meaning: With harm or loss to something else; also, paid for by someone.
usage: Pattern: achieve X at the expense of Y. Also: at someone's expense (a joke at his expense = making fun of him).
examples: The company grew at the expense of its workers' wellbeing.
Don't improve speed at the expense of accuracy.
They made jokes at my expense.
Economic growth shouldn't come at the expense of the environment.

meaning: For the reason that.
usage: Formal, common in legal and academic writing. Also: on the grounds of something (on the grounds of cost/safety).
examples: The plan was rejected on the grounds that it was too expensive.
He refused on the grounds that he had too much work.
The film was banned on the grounds that it was too violent.
She appealed on the grounds that the trial had been unfair.

meaning: In order to help, benefit, or achieve something; because of.
usage: Patterns: for the sake of something/someone; for someone's sake; for the sake of argument (to imagine a situation for discussion).
examples: For the sake of clarity, I've divided the essay into sections.
They stayed together for the sake of the children.
Let's assume, for the sake of argument, that prices double.
Don't change things just for the sake of it.

meaning: Considering or because of new information.
usage: British English also “in the light of”. Typical objects: new evidence/recent events/these findings.
examples: In light of recent events, the concert has been cancelled.
The policy was reviewed in light of new evidence.
In light of these findings, we recommend further research.
In the light of the weather forecast, we postponed the trip.

meaning: Using a particular method or tool.
usage: Formal. Common in academic descriptions of methods: “Data was collected by means of a questionnaire.”
examples: Data was collected by means of an online questionnaire.
The goods are transported by means of a conveyor belt.
They communicated by means of sign language.
The problem was solved by means of a simple formula.

meaning: Except for; not including.
usage: Formal. Pattern: With the exception of X, all/everyone… Also “with few exceptions”.
examples: With the exception of Sunday, the shop is open every day.
All the students passed, with the exception of two.
With the exception of the ending, I loved the film.
Every country, with the exception of one, signed the agreement.

meaning: Following or obeying a rule, law, or wish.
usage: Formal and common in official and legal writing. Typical objects: the law, regulations, guidelines, someone's wishes.
examples: The study was conducted in accordance with ethical guidelines.
Her ashes were scattered in accordance with her wishes.
All products are made in accordance with safety regulations.
Payment must be made in accordance with the contract.

meaning: Rather than; in contrast with.
usage: Used to make a clear contrast between two things. Common in speech and writing.
examples: I prefer reading novels, as opposed to non-fiction.
The course focuses on practice as opposed to theory.
Prices rose by five per cent, as opposed to two per cent last year.
We need long-term solutions as opposed to quick fixes.

meaning: Using something as the reason or main factor for a decision.
usage: Also: on the basis that… Typical objects: evidence, merit, experience, results. Similar: based on.
examples: Candidates are selected on the basis of merit.
Don't judge people on the basis of appearance.
The decision was made on the basis of the latest data.
Scholarships are awarded on the basis of academic results.

meaning: An explanation that seems reasonable and likely to be true.
usage: Verbs: offer/provide/find a plausible explanation for something. Also: the most plausible explanation is that…
examples: There must be a plausible explanation for the results.
The most plausible explanation is human error.
Scientists have offered several plausible explanations.
Can you give a plausible explanation for being late?

meaning: An explanation that makes people believe it is true.
usage: Verbs: give/provide/offer a convincing explanation. Often negative: “no convincing explanation”.
examples: Nobody has given a convincing explanation for the mystery.
She couldn't provide a convincing explanation for the missing money.
The theory offers a convincing explanation of the data.
His excuse was not a convincing explanation.

meaning: A description of events that includes many facts and details.
usage: Verbs: give/provide/write a detailed account of something. Also: a full/first-hand/eyewitness account.
examples: The book gives a detailed account of life during the war.
Police asked her for a detailed account of what happened.
The report provides a detailed account of the company's finances.
He wrote a detailed account of his travels in Asia.

meaning: A short statement of the main points of something.
usage: Verbs: give/provide/write a brief summary of something. Also: a short/concise summary; in summary.
examples: Begin your report with a brief summary of the findings.
Could you give me a brief summary of the meeting?
Each chapter ends with a brief summary.
Here is a brief summary of the main arguments.

meaning: To state the most important ideas of something briefly.
usage: British spelling also “summarise”. Common in instructions and conclusions: “In conclusion, let me summarize the main points.”
examples: In your conclusion, summarize the main points of your argument.
Let me summarize the main points of today's lecture.
Can you summarize the main points of the article in 100 words?
The speaker summarized the main points at the end.

meaning: To describe the main parts of something and how they are organized.
usage: Common in introductions: “This essay will first… and then…”. Also: outline a plan/proposal/the main ideas.
examples: The introduction should outline the structure of the essay.
Let me briefly outline the structure of the presentation.
The first chapter outlines the structure of the thesis.
She outlined the structure of the new department.

meaning: To organize the parts of an essay in a logical order.
usage: “Structure” is used as a verb here. Related: a well-structured essay; the structure of an argument.
examples: Learning how to structure an essay is an important skill.
A clear plan helps you structure your essay logically.
Most students structure an essay with an introduction, body, and conclusion.
Her essay was well structured and easy to follow.

meaning: A sentence, usually in the introduction, that states the main argument of an essay.
usage: Verbs: write/state/develop a thesis statement. Also: a clear/strong thesis statement. Common in academic writing instruction.
examples: Your thesis statement should appear at the end of the introduction.
A strong thesis statement makes your argument clear.
The teacher asked us to rewrite our thesis statements.
Every paragraph should support the thesis statement.

meaning: A sentence, usually at the start of a paragraph, that states its main idea.
usage: It is a key concept in paragraph writing. Supporting sentences then develop the topic sentence.
examples: Each paragraph should begin with a clear topic sentence.
The topic sentence tells the reader what the paragraph is about.
Her topic sentences are clear and well focused.
Underline the topic sentence in each paragraph.

meaning: A point or reason that helps prove a main argument.
usage: Also: supporting evidence/details/examples. Essays usually develop two or three supporting arguments.
examples: Each paragraph presents a supporting argument.
Back up every supporting argument with evidence.
Her essay has three strong supporting arguments.
The weakest supporting argument should come first or be removed.

meaning: To provide evidence that shows a claim is true.
usage: Pattern: back up a claim with evidence/data. Also: back up an argument/a statement. Formal synonym: substantiate.
examples: You need statistics to back up your claim.
He had no evidence to back up his claims.
Always back up a claim with examples.
The study backs up claims that exercise helps memory.

meaning: To state that something is true, often without proof.
usage: Patterns: make a claim that…/about something. Adjectives: a bold/false/unfounded/dubious claim. Also: make a claim for compensation (ask for money).
examples: The company made claims that its product cures headaches.
Don't make a claim you can't support.
He made bold claims about his abilities.
She made a claim for compensation after the accident.

meaning: To provide evidence that proves a claim is true.
usage: Formal. Often negative or passive: “The claim could not be substantiated.” Related: unsubstantiated claims.
examples: The journalist could not substantiate her claims.
Please provide documents to substantiate your claim.
Further research is needed to substantiate this claim.
None of the claims were substantiated.

meaning: A claim that is not supported by facts or evidence.
usage: Also: unfounded fears/rumours/allegations/accusations. Synonym: baseless.
examples: The minister dismissed the report as an unfounded claim.
Social media spreads many unfounded claims.
Her claim that the test was unfair turned out to be unfounded.
The company denied the unfounded claims against it.

meaning: A confident statement that may be difficult to prove.
usage: Verbs: make a bold claim. It can be admiring or sceptical: “That's a bold claim.”
examples: The author makes the bold claim that school is unnecessary.
That's a bold claim; can you prove it?
The company made a bold claim about its new battery.
Some scientists are sceptical of the bold claim.

meaning: A statement that is too general and ignores important exceptions.
usage: Verbs: make a sweeping statement. Similar: a sweeping generalization. Critical in tone.
examples: It's a sweeping statement to say all politicians are corrupt.
Avoid making sweeping statements in your essay.
Her sweeping statement about young people offended many.
That's rather a sweeping statement, don't you think?

meaning: A source of information that can be trusted.
usage: Also: a credible/reputable/trustworthy source. In journalism: “according to a reliable source”.
examples: Make sure you use reliable sources in your research.
Wikipedia isn't always a reliable source.
I heard from a reliable source that she's leaving.
Government statistics are usually a reliable source.

meaning: An original document or record from the time being studied, such as a letter, diary, or raw data.
usage: Opposite: a secondary source. Common in history and research methods.
examples: Diaries are an important primary source for historians.
The study relies on primary sources from the 18th century.
Interviews are a primary source of data.
Try to use primary sources wherever possible.

meaning: A work that analyses or interprets primary sources, such as a textbook or review article.
usage: Opposite: a primary source. Secondary sources are useful for overviews but further from original evidence.
examples: Textbooks are a secondary source.
The essay relies too heavily on secondary sources.
A secondary source can help you understand the context.
Check the secondary source against the original documents.

meaning: An academic publication that is respected and trusted.
usage: Also: a peer-reviewed/leading/prestigious journal. Verbs: publish in a reputable journal.
examples: The study was published in a reputable journal.
Only cite articles from reputable journals.
Getting published in a reputable journal is difficult.
The findings appeared in a reputable medical journal.

meaning: To have a piece of academic research printed or made available in a journal.
usage: Also: write/submit/present a paper. “Paper” here means an academic article.
examples: She published a paper on climate migration.
Researchers must publish papers to advance their careers.
The team published a paper in Nature.
He has published over fifty papers.

meaning: Research that has been evaluated by other experts in the field before publication.
usage: Also: a peer-reviewed journal/article/study. Considered more reliable than non-reviewed sources.
examples: The claims are not supported by peer-reviewed research.
Students should rely on peer-reviewed research.
Peer-reviewed research takes months to publish.
The article cites several pieces of peer-reviewed research.

meaning: Money given by an organization to pay for a research project.
usage: Verbs: apply for/win/receive/be awarded a research grant.
examples: She won a research grant to study coral reefs.
The university received a large research grant.
Applying for a research grant takes a lot of time.
The research grant covers three years of work.

meaning: To formally ask an organization to provide money for a project.
usage: Also: seek/secure/obtain/receive funding. “Funding” is uncountable.
examples: The team applied for funding from the government.
We need to apply for funding before the end of March.
Small charities often struggle to apply for funding.
She applied for funding to start her business.

meaning: A particular subject or area of knowledge that people study.
usage: Also: a field of research; in the field of medicine/linguistics. Synonym: discipline.
examples: Psychology is a relatively young field of study.
What's your field of study?
Artificial intelligence is a fast-growing field of study.
She changed her field of study after the first year.

meaning: A subject that someone knows a lot about.
usage: Pattern: someone's area of expertise; outside my area of expertise. Common when politely declining to comment.
examples: Tax law is her main area of expertise.
I'm afraid that question is outside my area of expertise.
Each member of the team has a different area of expertise.
What's your area of expertise?

meaning: One of the most important and respected specialists in a field.
usage: Pattern: a leading expert on/in something. Also: a leading figure/scientist/authority.
examples: She is a leading expert on climate change.
The book was reviewed by a leading expert in the field.
Leading experts warned against the policy.
He's considered a leading expert in Asian history.

meaning: A person recognized internationally as an expert on a subject.
usage: Pattern: a world authority on something. Also: a leading authority.
examples: He is a world authority on tropical diseases.
The professor is a world authority on Shakespeare.
She became a world authority on volcanoes.
The institute invited a world authority to give the lecture.

meaning: A study that introduces important new ideas or methods.
usage: Also: groundbreaking research/work/discovery. Similar: pioneering, innovative.
examples: A groundbreaking study showed the link between smoking and cancer.
Her groundbreaking study changed how we treat depression.
The team published a groundbreaking study on memory.
This groundbreaking study has been cited thousands of times.

meaning: The most advanced and modern research in a field.
usage: Also: cutting-edge technology/design/science. Hyphenated before a noun. Similar: state-of-the-art.
examples: The university is known for cutting-edge research in AI.
The lab carries out cutting-edge research on cancer.
Cutting-edge research requires expensive equipment.
Students can take part in cutting-edge research projects.

meaning: An important new discovery in science.
usage: Verbs: make/achieve/hail a scientific breakthrough. Also: a major/medical breakthrough.
examples: The vaccine was hailed as a scientific breakthrough.
Scientists have made a scientific breakthrough in battery technology.
Penicillin was one of the greatest scientific breakthroughs.
A scientific breakthrough could transform the industry.

meaning: To find something that was not known before.
usage: Adjectives: an important/major/remarkable/surprising discovery. Also: a discovery about/of something.
examples: Archaeologists made an important discovery near the river.
She made a surprising discovery while reading old letters.
Scientists made the discovery by accident.
We made the discovery that the data was incomplete.

meaning: To finish something by the time it is due.
usage: Also: work to/hit/make a deadline. Opposite: miss a deadline. Adjectives: a tight/strict deadline.
examples: We worked all night to meet the deadline.
Can you meet a Friday deadline?
The team always meets its deadlines.
It was a tight deadline, but we met it.

meaning: To fail to finish something by the time it is due.
usage: Opposite: meet a deadline. Common consequences: penalties, lost marks, lost contracts.
examples: If we miss this deadline, we'll lose the contract.
She missed the deadline by one day.
Students who miss a deadline lose ten per cent of their mark.
The project has already missed two deadlines.

meaning: To decide the date or time by which something must be finished.
usage: Pattern: set a deadline for something. Adjectives: a realistic/tight/strict deadline.
examples: The manager set a deadline of 30 June for the report.
It helps to set yourself a deadline for each task.
Did they set a deadline for applications?
Setting realistic deadlines reduces stress.

meaning: To allow more time to finish something than was originally agreed.
usage: Pattern: extend the deadline (by a week/to Friday). Also: ask for/get a deadline extension.
examples: The deadline has been extended by two weeks.
Could you extend the deadline until Monday?
The government extended the deadline for tax returns.
They refused to extend the deadline.

meaning: To organize and have a meeting.
usage: Also: have/arrange/schedule a meeting. Irregular: held. Often passive: “The meeting will be held in room 3.”
examples: We hold a team meeting every Monday morning.
The meeting will be held online.
The board held an emergency meeting last night.
Let's hold a meeting to discuss the budget.

meaning: To be in charge of a meeting and control the discussion.
usage: The person is the “chair” or “chairperson”. Related: chair a committee/discussion/debate.
examples: The director will chair the meeting.
She chaired the meeting very efficiently.
Who's chairing today's meeting?
It's difficult to chair a meeting when people keep interrupting.

meaning: To arrange a meeting and ask people to attend, often urgently.
usage: Also: call an emergency meeting; call a meeting for 3 p.m. Similar: convene a meeting (formal).
examples: The CEO called a meeting to discuss the crisis.
Let's call a meeting for tomorrow afternoon.
The union called an emergency meeting.
Why did they call a meeting at such short notice?

meaning: To be present at a meeting.
usage: Note: attend + object directly (not “attend to a meeting”, which means something else). Also: go to a meeting.
examples: All staff are required to attend the meeting.
I can't attend the meeting on Friday.
Over 200 people attended the meeting.
She attended the meeting via video link.

meaning: To decide the list of topics to be discussed; also, to decide what issues are most important.
usage: Also: draw up/circulate an agenda; be on the agenda. Figuratively: “The media sets the political agenda.”
examples: The chair sets the agenda for each meeting.
Who will set the agenda for the conference?
Big companies often set the agenda in their industries.
The media plays a big role in setting the political agenda.

meaning: To write the official notes of what is said and decided at a meeting.
usage: “Minutes” is plural in this sense. Also: circulate/approve the minutes.
examples: Could you take the minutes at today's meeting?
The secretary takes the minutes at every board meeting.
Who's taking the minutes?
I took the minutes at the board meeting last week.

meaning: To agree on something after discussion or negotiation.
usage: Also: come to/arrive at an agreement. Pattern: reach an agreement on/over something; reach an agreement with someone.
examples: The two companies reached an agreement on prices.
After weeks of talks, they finally reached an agreement.
We hope to reach an agreement with the union soon.
It took hours to reach an agreement.

meaning: To make an agreement with someone, especially in business.
usage: Pattern: strike a deal with someone. Irregular: struck. Informal to neutral. Similar: do/cut a deal.
examples: The company struck a deal with a Japanese supplier.
They struck a deal worth $10 million.
We managed to strike a deal at the last minute.
The two parties struck a deal to form a government.

meaning: To successfully complete a business agreement.
usage: Also: clinch/seal a deal. Common in sales: “a closer” is good at closing deals.
examples: She closed the deal over dinner.
We're hoping to close the deal by the end of the month.
Good salespeople know how to close a deal.
The deal was closed after months of negotiation.

meaning: To formally complete an agreement so that it is final.
usage: Often used with “handshake”: “They sealed the deal with a handshake.” Similar: close/clinch a deal.
examples: They sealed the deal with a handshake.
A signed contract will seal the deal.
The free delivery offer sealed the deal for me.
The two companies sealed a deal to build a new factory.

meaning: To discuss the terms of a formal agreement in order to reach a deal.
usage: Also: renegotiate a contract (discuss it again to change it). Related: negotiate a deal/salary/settlement.
examples: Her agent negotiated a new contract with the club.
It took six months to negotiate the contract.
The union is negotiating a contract for its members.
Lawyers spent weeks negotiating the contract for the merger.

meaning: To write your name on a formal agreement to show that you accept it.
usage: Pattern: sign a contract with someone. Related: draw up/terminate/breach a contract.
examples: She signed a two-year contract with a publisher.
Read the contract carefully before you sign it.
The player signed a contract worth £5 million.
We signed the contract last week.

meaning: To formally end a contract before it is completed.
usage: Formal. Pattern: terminate a contract with someone. Related: termination clause; early termination fee.
examples: The company terminated his contract without notice.
Either party can terminate the contract with 30 days' notice.
They terminated the contract because of poor performance.
Terminating the contract early will incur a fee.

meaning: A failure to do what was agreed in a contract.
usage: Patterns: be in breach of contract; sue someone for breach of contract. The verb form is “breach a contract”.
examples: The supplier was sued for breach of contract.
Failing to deliver on time is a breach of contract.
The company is in breach of contract.
She won damages for breach of contract.

meaning: To formally give a plan or suggestion to someone for consideration.
usage: Also: put forward/present/approve/reject a proposal. Common in business and grant applications.
examples: Three companies submitted proposals for the project.
Please submit your proposal by the end of the month.
We submitted a proposal for a new marketing strategy.
She submitted a proposal to reorganize the sales team.

meaning: To try to persuade someone to buy something, invest, or accept an idea.
usage: Pattern: make a pitch to someone/for something. Related: a sales pitch; pitch an idea. Start-ups make pitches to investors.
examples: The start-up made a pitch to a group of investors.
She made a strong pitch for more funding.
Each team had five minutes to make a pitch.
He made a pitch for the job by showing his portfolio.

meaning: To be chosen to provide goods or services under a formal agreement.
usage: Also: secure/land/be awarded a contract. Irregular: won. Opposite: lose a contract.
examples: The firm won a contract to build a new bridge.
We're hoping to win the contract with the hospital.
They won a £20 million government contract.
Winning the contract saved hundreds of jobs.

meaning: To introduce a new product to the market.
usage: Related: a product launch; launch a campaign/website/service. Often passive: “The phone will be launched in May.”
examples: The company will launch a new product next month.
Apple launches products at special events.
Before you launch a product, test it with real users.
The product was launched in 15 countries at once.

meaning: To start selling products or services in a particular market.
usage: Also: break into/penetrate a market. Related: market entry; barriers to entry.
examples: The company plans to enter the Vietnamese market next year.
Many start-ups struggle to enter the market.
New competitors have entered the market.
It's expensive to enter the electric car market.

meaning: To increase the percentage of total sales in a market that a company has.
usage: Also: increase/lose/win market share. Market share is often expressed as a percentage.
examples: The brand has gained market share in Asia.
Cutting prices helped the company gain market share.
Electric cars are steadily gaining market share.
Smaller brands are gaining market share from the industry leaders.

meaning: An advantage that helps a person or company do better than competitors.
usage: Verbs: give/have/gain/maintain a competitive edge. Pattern: a competitive edge over someone.
examples: Speaking several languages gives you a competitive edge.
The company's technology gives it a competitive edge.
Small businesses need a competitive edge to survive.
Innovation helps maintain a competitive edge.

meaning: A feature that makes a company or product better than competitors.
usage: Pattern: a competitive advantage over someone. A key concept in business strategy (e.g. lower costs, better quality).
examples: Low production costs give the firm a competitive advantage.
Customer service can be a major competitive advantage.
What is our competitive advantage over other brands?
Their location gives them a competitive advantage.

meaning: A small, specialized market for a particular product or service.
usage: Verbs: target/serve/find a niche market. “Niche” is pronounced /niːʃ/ or /nɪtʃ/.
examples: The company targets a niche market of vegan athletes.
Small businesses often succeed by serving a niche market.
Luxury watches are a niche market.
They found a niche market for eco-friendly packaging.

meaning: The particular group of customers a business aims to sell to.
usage: Also: target audience/customers. Verbs: identify/define/reach a target market.
examples: Our target market is young professionals.
You need to identify your target market before advertising.
The product failed because it didn't appeal to its target market.
Students are the main target market for this app.

meaning: The collection and analysis of information about what customers want and need.
usage: Verbs: carry out/conduct/do market research. It is uncountable.
examples: We carried out market research before launching the product.
Market research shows that customers want cheaper options.
The company spends a lot on market research.
According to market research, the brand is popular with teenagers.

meaning: An opportunity to sell a product or service that people need but no one is providing.
usage: Verbs: spot/see/identify/fill a gap in the market.
examples: She spotted a gap in the market for healthy fast food.
The app fills a gap in the market.
There's a gap in the market for affordable childcare.
Successful entrepreneurs know how to identify a gap in the market.

meaning: To gain control of most of the sales of a particular product.
usage: Pattern: corner the market in/on something. It often suggests dominance or even unfair control.
examples: The company has cornered the market in smartphone chips.
They tried to corner the market by buying up all the stock.
One brand has cornered the market for luxury handbags.
It's hard for new companies when one firm has cornered the market.

meaning: A market in which there are so many products that it is hard to sell more.
usage: Also: the market is saturated; market saturation. Common in discussions of competition.
examples: The coffee shop industry is a saturated market.
It's difficult to succeed in a saturated market.
The smartphone market is becoming saturated.
In a saturated market, branding becomes crucial.

meaning: To increase the amount of goods sold.
usage: Also: increase/drive/raise sales. “Boost” also collocates with the economy, confidence, morale, productivity.
examples: The advertising campaign boosted sales by 20 per cent.
Discounts can boost sales in the short term.
The new design helped boost sales.
Shops hope the holidays will boost sales.

meaning: To produce income for a business or government.
usage: Also: generate income/profit/sales. Common in business and public finance.
examples: Advertising generates most of the website's revenue.
Tourism generates significant revenue for the city.
We need new ways to generate revenue.
The tax is expected to generate £2 billion in revenue.

meaning: To reduce the amount of money spent.
usage: Also: reduce/lower/slash costs; cost-cutting measures. Irregular: cut, cut, cut.
examples: The company cut costs by closing two offices.
We need to cut costs without reducing quality.
Many firms cut costs during the recession.
Working from home helped us cut costs.

meaning: To lower the regular costs of running a business, such as rent and electricity.
usage: “Overheads” (British, plural) / “overhead” (American). Also: cut/keep down overheads.
examples: Moving to a smaller office helped reduce overheads.
Online shops reduce overheads by avoiding expensive high-street rents.
The company is trying to reduce overheads by going paperless.
Remote work can significantly reduce overheads.

meaning: To make more money after costs have been paid.
usage: Also: boost/maximize profits; profits rise/fall. Related: a profit margin; pre-tax profits.
examples: The new strategy increased profits by 15 per cent.
Companies try to increase profits by cutting costs.
Automation helped the factory increase profits.
Raising prices doesn't always increase profits.

meaning: To earn more money than you spend.
usage: Also: turn/earn a profit; make a profit on something. Opposite: make a loss.
examples: The café made a profit in its first year.
We made a small profit on the sale of the house.
Many start-ups take years to make a profit.
The company hasn't made a profit since 2019.

meaning: To spend more money than you earn.
usage: British English; American English often says “take a loss” or “lose money”. Also: suffer/report a loss.
examples: The airline made a loss for the third year in a row.
We made a loss on the event because few people came.
The company expects to make a loss this quarter.
Many restaurants make a loss in their first year.

meaning: To earn exactly as much money as you spend, making neither a profit nor a loss.
usage: Related noun: the break-even point. Irregular: broke, broken.
examples: The business expects to break even next year.
We barely broke even on the concert.
How many tickets do we need to sell to break even?
The company finally broke even after three years.

meaning: To start making more money than you spend.
usage: It often implies success after a difficult period. Similar: make a profit; be in the black.
examples: The start-up turned a profit for the first time last quarter.
It took the restaurant two years to turn a profit.
Investors want to know when the company will turn a profit.
Despite rising sales, the firm has yet to turn a profit.

meaning: The difference between the cost of producing something and the price it is sold for, usually as a percentage.
usage: Adjectives: a high/low/narrow/healthy profit margin. Also simply “margins”: “Margins are tight.”
examples: Supermarkets operate on a low profit margin.
Luxury goods have a high profit margin.
Rising costs have squeezed our profit margin.
The company aims to increase its profit margin to 20 per cent.

meaning: A situation in which a business does not have enough money coming in to pay its bills on time.
usage: Also: cash flow difficulties; manage/improve cash flow. A profitable business can still have cash flow problems.
examples: Late payments caused a cash flow problem for the small business.
Many start-ups fail because of cash flow problems.
The company took out a loan to solve its cash flow problem.
Careful planning can prevent a cash flow problem.

meaning: A limited amount of money that must be managed carefully.
usage: Patterns: be on a tight budget; work to/within a tight budget. Also used in everyday life.
examples: The film was made on a tight budget.
We're working to a tight budget this year.
With a tight budget, every expense must be justified.
Students often live on a tight budget.

meaning: To spend no more than the amount of money planned.
usage: Also: keep within budget; come in under budget. Opposite: go over budget.
examples: The project stayed within budget and finished on time.
It's hard to stay within budget when prices keep rising.
We need to stay within budget this quarter.
The team managed to stay within budget despite delays.

meaning: To spend more money than was planned.
usage: Also: run over budget; exceed the budget. Opposite: stay within/come in under budget.
examples: The new stadium went over budget by £50 million.
Most building projects go over budget.
We can't afford to go over budget again.
The film went way over budget.

meaning: To decide how money, people, or equipment will be shared and used.
usage: Pattern: allocate resources to something/for something. Also: allocate funds/time/staff. The noun is “resource allocation”.
examples: Managers must allocate resources efficiently.
The government allocated more resources to healthcare.
We need to allocate resources to the most urgent projects.
Poorly allocated resources lead to waste.

meaning: The profit or benefit gained from an investment compared with its cost.
usage: Often shortened to ROI. Adjectives: a good/high/low/positive return on investment.
examples: The new software delivered a good return on investment.
Investors expect a high return on investment.
Training staff gives a strong return on investment.
What return on investment can we expect from this campaign?

meaning: To make people or companies want to put money into a business or place.
usage: Also: attract foreign/private investment; attract investors. Common in economic development.
examples: The government cut taxes to attract foreign investment.
The region has struggled to attract investment.
Good infrastructure helps attract investment.
The start-up attracted investment from several big firms.

meaning: To obtain money needed to start or develop a business.
usage: Also: raise money/funds/finance. Methods include loans, selling shares, and crowdfunding.
examples: The company raised capital by selling shares.
Start-ups often struggle to raise capital.
They raised capital through crowdfunding.
We need to raise capital before we can expand.

meaning: A share in a business or an interest in something's success.
usage: Patterns: have/hold/buy/sell a stake in something; a 20 per cent stake. Figuratively: have a stake in the outcome (care because it affects you).
examples: The bank bought a 30 per cent stake in the company.
He sold his stake in the business for millions.
Local residents have a stake in the future of the town.
Employees hold a small stake in the firm.

meaning: A document describing a business's goals and how it will achieve them, especially financially.
usage: Verbs: write/draw up/present a business plan. Investors and banks usually require one.
examples: You need a clear business plan to get a bank loan.
She spent months writing her business plan.
Investors were impressed by the business plan.
A good business plan includes financial forecasts.

meaning: A short statement of an organization's purpose and values.
usage: Verbs: write/draft/publish a mission statement. Sometimes criticized as vague corporate language.
examples: The company's mission statement focuses on sustainability.
Our mission statement is printed on every office wall.
A mission statement should be short and clear.
Employees helped write the new mission statement.

meaning: A plan designed to achieve goals over many years.
usage: Verbs: develop/adopt/implement a long-term strategy. Opposite: a short-term fix.
examples: The company needs a long-term strategy for growth.
Investing in staff is part of our long-term strategy.
Without a long-term strategy, businesses drift.
The government has no long-term strategy on housing.

meaning: An important decision made to achieve long-term goals.
usage: Verbs: make/take a strategic decision. Also: a strategic plan/move/partnership/goal.
examples: Moving production to Vietnam was a strategic decision.
The board made a strategic decision to focus on online sales.
Strategic decisions are usually made by senior managers.
It was a strategic decision to delay the product launch.

meaning: To put a planned approach into action.
usage: Also: implement a plan/policy/change. Related: develop/adopt/execute a strategy.
examples: The new CEO implemented a strategy to reduce costs.
It's easy to plan a strategy but harder to implement it.
The strategy was implemented across all branches.
We need more staff to implement the strategy successfully.

meaning: To decide specific results that someone should achieve.
usage: Also: set goals/objectives. Adjectives: realistic/ambitious/sales targets.
examples: Managers set targets for each member of the sales team.
It's important to set realistic targets.
The government set targets for reducing emissions.
We set ambitious targets for next year.

meaning: To achieve a planned result or level.
usage: Also: meet/reach/achieve a target. Opposite: miss a target. Irregular: hit, hit, hit.
examples: The team hit its sales target a month early.
If we hit our target, everyone gets a bonus.
The company failed to hit its growth target.
We're on track to hit our target this year.

meaning: To achieve more than the planned results.
usage: Also: beat/surpass targets; exceed expectations. Often used in performance reviews.
examples: She exceeded her sales targets every quarter.
The project exceeded all its targets.
Staff who exceed targets receive a bonus.
We exceeded our fundraising targets by 20 per cent.

meaning: Measurable values that show how well a company or employee is achieving its goals.
usage: Often abbreviated to KPIs. Verbs: set/track/measure/meet KPIs. Common in management.
examples: Customer satisfaction is one of our key performance indicators.
The manager reviews key performance indicators every month.
Key performance indicators help track progress towards goals.
Each department has its own key performance indicators.

meaning: A meeting in which a manager evaluates an employee's work.
usage: Also: an appraisal, an annual review. Verbs: have/conduct/carry out a performance review.
examples: I have my performance review next week.
Managers conduct performance reviews twice a year.
The performance review highlighted areas for improvement.
She got excellent feedback in her performance review.

meaning: A yearly formal assessment of an employee's work and development.
usage: British English. Similar: performance review. Verbs: have/carry out an annual appraisal.
examples: We discussed my career goals at my annual appraisal.
All staff have an annual appraisal with their manager.
Pay rises are linked to the annual appraisal.
Prepare examples of your achievements before your annual appraisal.

meaning: To formally talk to a group of people about a subject, often with slides.
usage: Also: make/deliver a presentation; a presentation on/about something. Irregular: gave, given.
examples: I have to give a presentation to the board tomorrow.
She gave an excellent presentation on market trends.
Students give presentations in English every week.
Giving a presentation makes many people nervous.

meaning: To present a talk formally to an audience.
usage: More formal than “give a presentation”. Also: deliver a speech/lecture/talk.
examples: The CEO delivered a presentation on the company's future.
He delivered the presentation confidently.
Practise before you deliver a presentation.
She delivered a powerful presentation at the conference.

meaning: To formally ask to be considered for a job, usually by sending an application.
usage: Also: apply for a position/post/role. Related: a job application; an applicant.
examples: I've applied for a job in marketing.
She applied for over fifty jobs after graduating.
You can apply for the job online.
Make sure your CV is up to date before you apply for a job.

meaning: A formal request to be considered for a job, usually including a form, CV, and cover letter.
usage: Verbs: submit/fill in/complete/send a job application. Also: application form.
examples: I've sent off ten job applications this week.
Fill in the job application carefully.
Spelling mistakes can ruin a job application.
Her job application was rejected without explanation.

meaning: A formal meeting in which an employer asks questions to decide whether to hire someone.
usage: Verbs: have/attend/go for/prepare for a job interview. Also: interview for a job; be invited to an interview.
examples: I have a job interview tomorrow morning.
Prepare answers to common questions before a job interview.
She was nervous before her first job interview.
The job interview lasted over an hour.

meaning: A letter sent with a CV explaining why you are suitable for a job.
usage: Also: a covering letter (British). Verbs: write/attach/send a cover letter.
examples: Always send a cover letter with your CV.
Tailor your cover letter to each job.
Her cover letter impressed the recruiter.
A good cover letter is no longer than one page.

meaning: To choose a small number of the best applicants for further consideration.
usage: “Shortlist” is both a verb and a noun: be on the shortlist; be shortlisted for a job/prize.
examples: We shortlisted five candidates for interview.
Only shortlisted candidates will be contacted.
The panel shortlisted three candidates for the final round.
It took a week to shortlist candidates from 200 applications.

meaning: To employ new workers.
usage: Also: recruit/take on staff. Opposite: lay off/dismiss staff. In British English “hire” is also used for renting things.
examples: The restaurant is hiring staff for the summer.
We need to hire more staff to cope with demand.
Small firms find it expensive to hire staff.
The company hired 50 new staff last year.

meaning: To find and employ skilled people.
usage: Also: attract/retain/nurture talent; top talent. “Talent” here means talented people (uncountable).
examples: Tech companies compete to recruit talent.
Flexible working helps businesses recruit talent.
The firm recruits talent from top universities.
It's becoming harder to recruit talent in the industry.

meaning: A formal proposal from an employer to give someone a job.
usage: Verbs: receive/get/accept/turn down a job offer. Also: an offer letter.
examples: She received a job offer from a bank in Singapore.
I'm still waiting for a job offer.
He had two job offers and couldn't decide.
The job offer included a generous salary.

meaning: To agree to take something that has been offered, such as a job or a price.
usage: Opposite: turn down/decline/reject an offer. Also: accept a job/an invitation/a proposal.
examples: She accepted the offer immediately.
We've accepted an offer on our house.
Before you accept an offer, check the contract carefully.
He accepted the offer of a promotion.

meaning: To refuse something that has been offered.
usage: Pattern: turn an offer down / turn down an offer. More formal: decline an offer. Also: turn down an invitation/a request.
examples: She turned down an offer from a big law firm.
Why did you turn down the offer?
He turned the offer down because the pay was too low.
It was hard to turn down such a good offer.

meaning: To discuss with an employer how much you will be paid.
usage: Also: negotiate a pay rise/package. Related: salary negotiation.
examples: Don't be afraid to negotiate a salary.
She negotiated a higher salary than she expected.
Research typical pay before you negotiate a salary.
Many graduates don't negotiate their starting salary.

meaning: The amount someone is paid when they first begin a job.
usage: Adjectives: a competitive/generous/low starting salary. Pattern: a starting salary of £25,000.
examples: The job offers a starting salary of £30,000.
Engineers usually have a high starting salary.
She negotiated a better starting salary.
Starting salaries in teaching are relatively low.

meaning: An increase in the amount of money someone is paid.
usage: British English; American English: “a raise”. Verbs: get/ask for/be given/award a pay rise.
examples: I asked my boss for a pay rise.
Nurses were given a five per cent pay rise.
She got a pay rise after her promotion.
Staff haven't had a pay rise for three years.

meaning: To be given a higher position at work.
usage: Also: be promoted (to a position). The noun is “promotion”: get/earn/be up for a promotion.
examples: She got promoted to senior manager.
It took him five years to get promoted.
Hard work alone won't always help you get promoted.
He got promoted after just one year.

meaning: To progress to higher positions in your job over time.
usage: Also: move up/rise up the career ladder; the corporate ladder. Informal and metaphorical.
examples: She climbed the career ladder quickly.
Many people sacrifice free time to climb the career ladder.
Climbing the career ladder isn't everyone's goal.
Women still face barriers as they climb the career ladder.

meaning: The series of jobs and progress someone makes in their working life.
usage: Verbs: choose/follow/pursue a career path. Also: a career change/goal/move.
examples: She chose a career path in medicine.
Not everyone follows a traditional career path.
The company offers a clear career path for graduates.
He changed his career path at forty.

meaning: A period of time away from work, for example to travel, study, or care for family.
usage: Verbs: take a career break. Common in discussions of parenting and work-life balance.
examples: She took a career break to raise her children.
Many people take a career break to travel.
After a two-year career break, he returned to teaching.
Employers are becoming more accepting of career breaks.

meaning: The likelihood that someone will keep their job.
usage: Uncountable. Collocations: offer/provide job security; lack of job security. Opposite: job insecurity.
examples: Government jobs usually offer good job security.
Many young workers have little job security.
She values job security more than a high salary.
Automation threatens job security in some industries.

meaning: The feeling of enjoyment and fulfilment that someone gets from their work.
usage: Uncountable. Adjectives: high/low job satisfaction. Common in HR and psychology research.
examples: Teachers often report high job satisfaction despite low pay.
Job satisfaction is more important to me than money.
Flexible working can improve job satisfaction.
Low job satisfaction leads to high staff turnover.

meaning: A large amount of work that someone has to do.
usage: Also: an increased/excessive/manageable workload. Verbs: cope with/reduce a heavy workload.
examples: Nurses are struggling with a heavy workload.
I have a heavy workload this week.
A heavy workload can lead to burnout.
The company hired extra staff to reduce the heavy workload.

meaning: To work extra hours beyond your normal working time.
usage: Also: do overtime; be paid overtime; unpaid overtime.
examples: I've been working overtime to finish the project.
Staff are paid extra if they work overtime.
Many teachers work overtime without extra pay.
She refused to work overtime every weekend.

meaning: A regular office job with standard working hours.
usage: Often used to contrast routine employment with flexible or creative work. Also: a nine-to-five.
examples: He quit his nine-to-five job to become a freelancer.
A nine-to-five job gives you evenings and weekends free.
Not everyone wants a nine-to-five job.
She was bored with her nine-to-five job.

meaning: A job in which you work the standard number of hours per week.
usage: Also: a full-time job/role/post. Opposite: a part-time position. As an adverb: work full-time.
examples: She was offered a full-time position after her internship.
We're advertising a full-time position in marketing.
A full-time position comes with paid holidays.
He's looking for a full-time position in IT.

meaning: A job in which you work fewer than the standard hours.
usage: Also: work part-time. Common for students and parents.
examples: Many students have a part-time job.
She works a part-time job in a café.
A part-time job helps pay for university.
He got a part-time job at the weekend.

meaning: An employment agreement for a limited period of time.
usage: Also: a fixed-term/short-term contract. Opposite: a permanent contract.
examples: She's on a temporary contract until December.
Many young workers are employed on temporary contracts.
A temporary contract offers little job security.
His temporary contract was extended for six months.

meaning: A job with no fixed end date.
usage: Also: a permanent job/post/contract. Opposite: a temporary position.
examples: After a year, she was offered a permanent position.
Permanent positions are hard to find in this industry.
He applied for a permanent position at the university.
A permanent position gives you more security.

meaning: In an initial trial period at a new job during which your performance is assessed.
usage: Also: a probation(ary) period. In legal contexts, “on probation” means released from prison under supervision.
examples: New employees are on probation for three months.
She's still on probation, so she can't take holiday yet.
He was dismissed while on probation.
During the probation period, either side can end the contract.

meaning: To formally tell your employer that you are going to leave your job.
usage: British English. Also: give/serve notice; work your notice (work the remaining period).
examples: I handed in my notice yesterday.
She handed in her notice after ten years.
You must hand in your notice a month before leaving.
He handed in his notice to start his own business.

meaning: To officially leave a job or position.
usage: Pattern: resign from a job/post/the board; resign as director. The noun is “resignation”.
examples: She resigned from her job to travel.
The minister resigned from the government after the scandal.
He resigned from the board last year.
Several staff resigned from the company in protest.

meaning: To lose your job because your employer no longer needs your position.
usage: British English; American English often says “be laid off”. Related: redundancy pay.
examples: He was made redundant when the factory closed.
Hundreds of workers will be made redundant.
She was made redundant after twenty years.
Being made redundant was a shock, but it led to a new career.

meaning: To end workers' employment, usually because there is not enough work or money.
usage: Pattern: lay off staff / lay staff off. Irregular: laid. Noun: layoffs.
examples: The company laid off 200 staff last month.
Restaurants were forced to lay off staff during the lockdown.
They had to lay off staff to cut costs.
The factory will lay off staff if orders fall.

meaning: Someone who works well with others in a group.
usage: Common in job adverts and CVs: “We're looking for a team player.” It is a compliment.
examples: We're looking for a team player with strong communication skills.
She's a real team player who always helps others.
Being a team player is essential in this role.
He's talented, but he's not a team player.

meaning: An awareness that you should do your duties and take care of things.
usage: Verbs: have/develop/show a sense of responsibility. Also: a sense of duty/purpose.
examples: Having a part-time job gave him a sense of responsibility.
She has a strong sense of responsibility towards her team.
Parents want children to develop a sense of responsibility.
A sense of responsibility is important in leadership.

meaning: To accept that you are in charge of something or to blame for something.
usage: Patterns: take (full) responsibility for something/doing something. Also: accept/claim responsibility.
examples: The manager took responsibility for the mistake.
You need to take responsibility for your own learning.
Who will take responsibility for the project?
She took full responsibility for the error.

meaning: To act before others do, without being told.
usage: Pattern: take the initiative (in doing something/to do something). It is valued in workplaces.
examples: She took the initiative and organized the training herself.
Employers want people who take the initiative.
Don't wait to be asked; take the initiative.
He took the initiative in contacting new clients.

meaning: To give some of your work to other people.
usage: Pattern: delegate tasks to someone. Also: delegate responsibility/authority. A key management skill.
examples: Good managers know how to delegate tasks.
She delegated tasks to the junior staff.
If you don't delegate tasks, you'll burn out.
Learning to delegate tasks made him more productive.

meaning: To make sure people have realistic ideas about what will happen or be achieved.
usage: Common in business and project management. Also: manage client/customer expectations.
examples: It's important to manage expectations from the start.
We need to manage the client's expectations about the deadline.
Good project managers manage expectations carefully.
The company managed expectations by announcing delays early.

meaning: To provide what clients require.
usage: Also: meet customer needs/demands/requirements. Related: tailor services to client needs.
examples: Our services are designed to meet client needs.
We adapt our products to meet client needs.
The team works hard to meet client needs quickly.
Failing to meet client needs can damage your reputation.

meaning: How happy customers are with a company's products or services.
usage: Uncountable. Collocations: improve/measure customer satisfaction; a customer satisfaction survey.
examples: Customer satisfaction is our top priority.
The survey measures customer satisfaction.
Faster delivery has improved customer satisfaction.
Customer satisfaction fell after the price rise.

meaning: The help and advice a company gives to its customers.
usage: Uncountable. Collocations: excellent/poor customer service; a customer service department/representative.
examples: The hotel is famous for its excellent customer service.
I called customer service about my order.
Poor customer service drives customers away.
She works in customer service at a bank.

meaning: A customer who keeps buying from the same company over time.
usage: Related: customer loyalty; loyalty card/programme. Businesses reward loyal customers.
examples: As a loyal customer, she receives special discounts.
It's cheaper to keep a loyal customer than to find a new one.
The café has many loyal customers.
Good service turns new buyers into loyal customers.

meaning: To keep existing customers rather than losing them to competitors.
usage: Related: customer retention. Also: retain staff/talent.
examples: Loyalty programmes help businesses retain customers.
It's hard to retain customers in a competitive market.
The company improved its service to retain customers.
Retaining customers costs less than attracting new ones.

meaning: All the customers who regularly buy from a business.
usage: Adjectives: a large/loyal/growing/diverse customer base. Verbs: build/expand a customer base.
examples: The company has a loyal customer base.
We want to expand our customer base in Asia.
Social media helped build a large customer base.
The brand has a young customer base.

meaning: To deal with a customer's complaint.
usage: Also: deal with/respond to/resolve a complaint. Related: make/file/lodge a complaint (customer).
examples: Staff are trained to handle complaints politely.
She handled the complaint professionally.
How should we handle a complaint about late delivery?
A manager will handle your complaint.

meaning: To take action to solve a problem that a customer has complained about.
usage: Irregular: dealt. Also: deal with a problem/an issue/a customer.
examples: The company dealt with my complaint quickly.
Who deals with complaints in this department?
Your complaint will be dealt with within five days.
She's very good at dealing with complaints.

meaning: To find a solution to a problem.
usage: Also: resolve a problem/dispute/conflict. More formal than “sort out” or “fix”.
examples: The technician resolved the issue in minutes.
We're working hard to resolve the issue.
The two departments met to resolve the issue.
If the issue isn't resolved, contact the manager.

meaning: To take further action about something, for example checking progress or responding.
usage: Pattern: follow up on something (a request/an email/a lead). Also: follow up with someone. Noun: a follow-up.
examples: I'm writing to follow up on our meeting last week.
Please follow up on the client's request.
She followed up on the job application with a phone call.
We need to follow up on these leads.

meaning: To keep someone informed about what is happening.
usage: Informal business English. Opposite: leave someone out of the loop.
examples: Please keep me in the loop about any changes.
We'll keep you in the loop as the project develops.
She felt nobody was keeping her in the loop.
Copy me on the emails to keep me in the loop.

meaning: To briefly contact someone to exchange information.
usage: Pattern: touch base with someone. Informal business jargon.
examples: Let's touch base next week about the project.
I just wanted to touch base before the meeting.
She touches base with her team every morning.
Can we touch base later today?

meaning: A phone call in which several people in different places take part.
usage: Verbs: have/hold/join/set up a conference call. Increasingly replaced by video calls.
examples: We have a conference call with the New York office at 3 p.m.
I joined the conference call late.
The conference call lasted two hours.
Can you set up a conference call for tomorrow?

meaning: A call in which people can see each other through cameras.
usage: Verbs: make/have/join a video call. Also: video conference.
examples: We had a video call with clients in Japan.
I speak to my parents on a video call every week.
The interview was conducted by video call.
Turn on your camera when you join a video call.

meaning: To send an answer to an email.
usage: Also: respond to/answer an email. “Reply” needs “to” before the object.
examples: Sorry for the delay in replying to your email.
Please reply to this email by Friday.
She replies to emails within an hour.
I forgot to reply to his email.

meaning: To send an email you have received to someone else.
usage: Pattern: forward an email to someone. Related: “I'll forward you the details.”
examples: Could you forward the email to the rest of the team?
I've forwarded the email to my manager.
Please forward me the email with the invitation.
Don't forward emails that contain private information.

meaning: To add a document to an email.
usage: Common email phrases: “Please find attached…”, “I've attached the file.”
examples: I've attached the file you requested.
Please attach the file as a PDF.
You forgot to attach the file!
The attached file contains the full report.

meaning: A short message to help someone remember something.
usage: Common email opener: “Just a quick reminder that…”. Also: a friendly/gentle reminder.
examples: Just a quick reminder that the meeting starts at 10.
I sent the team a quick reminder about the deadline.
Here's a quick reminder to submit your timesheets.
A quick reminder: the office is closed on Monday.

meaning: To arrange a time for a meeting.
usage: Also: arrange/set up/organize a meeting. Pattern: schedule a meeting for Tuesday/with someone.
examples: Let's schedule a meeting for next Tuesday.
I've scheduled a meeting with the client.
It's hard to schedule a meeting across time zones.
Could you schedule a meeting with the design team?

meaning: To change the time or date of a meeting.
usage: Also: move/rearrange a meeting. Pattern: reschedule for Thursday/to a later date.
examples: Could we reschedule the meeting for Thursday?
The meeting has been rescheduled to next week.
I need to reschedule our meeting; something urgent came up.
They rescheduled the meeting three times.

meaning: To delay a meeting until a later time.
usage: Also: put off a meeting (informal). Opposite: bring forward a meeting.
examples: The meeting has been postponed until next month.
We had to postpone the meeting because the director was ill.
Let's postpone the meeting until we have more data.
They postponed the meeting at the last minute.

meaning: A plan with very little free time between activities.
usage: Patterns: be on a tight schedule; work to a tight schedule. Also: a busy/packed schedule.
examples: We're on a tight schedule, so let's keep it short.
The project has a very tight schedule.
With such a tight schedule, any delay is a problem.
The band is touring on a tight schedule.

meaning: Earlier than planned.
usage: Opposite: behind schedule. Also: on schedule (as planned).
examples: The bridge was finished ahead of schedule.
We're two weeks ahead of schedule.
The project is running ahead of schedule.
Finishing ahead of schedule saved the company money.

meaning: Later than planned.
usage: Patterns: be/run/fall behind schedule. Opposite: ahead of schedule.
examples: The project is three months behind schedule.
Our train was running behind schedule.
Construction fell behind schedule because of bad weather.
We can't afford to get behind schedule.

meaning: Making progress as planned and likely to succeed.
usage: Patterns: be on track to do something; keep/get something back on track. Opposite: off track.
examples: We're on track to finish by June.
The project is back on track after some delays.
Sales are on track to reach record levels.
A clear plan keeps you on track.

meaning: A person responsible for planning and running a project.
usage: Related: project management; manage a project. A common job title.
examples: The project manager set clear deadlines.
She works as a project manager in construction.
Talk to the project manager about the budget.
A good project manager keeps everyone informed.

meaning: The gradual, uncontrolled growth of a project's goals beyond what was originally agreed.
usage: Uncountable. Verbs: avoid/prevent/manage scope creep. Common in project management.
examples: Scope creep caused the project to go over budget.
A clear contract helps prevent scope creep.
Every extra feature request contributes to scope creep.
The team struggled with scope creep from the client.

meaning: A short report on the current state of a task or project.
usage: Verbs: give/send/post/request a status update. Also used for social media posts.
examples: Please send me a status update by the end of the day.
Each team member gives a status update at the start of the meeting.
The client asked for a status update.
I'll post a status update on the project channel.

meaning: A document that describes how much work has been done on a project.
usage: Verbs: write/submit/give a progress report. Also: a monthly/weekly progress report.
examples: We submit a progress report every month.
The progress report shows we are on track.
The funding body requires a progress report.
She wrote a detailed progress report for the board.

meaning: A financial or progress report produced every three months.
usage: Related: quarterly results/earnings; the first/second quarter. Common in finance and corporate news.
examples: The company's quarterly report showed rising profits.
Shareholders are waiting for the quarterly report.
We prepare a quarterly report for the board.
The quarterly report will be published next week.

meaning: A yearly document in which a company or organization describes its activities and finances.
usage: Verbs: publish/release/prepare an annual report. Public companies must publish one.
examples: The charity published its annual report online.
According to the annual report, revenue grew by 10 per cent.
Investors read the annual report carefully.
The annual report includes a message from the CEO.

meaning: Formal records of a company's financial activities, such as income, assets, and debts.
usage: Usually plural. They include the balance sheet, income statement, and cash flow statement. Verbs: prepare/audit/publish financial statements.
examples: The auditors reviewed the financial statements.
Companies must publish financial statements every year.
Investors analyse financial statements before buying shares.
The financial statements revealed serious debts.

meaning: A financial statement showing a company's assets, liabilities, and equity at a particular time.
usage: Figuratively: “a strong balance sheet” means good financial health.
examples: The balance sheet shows the company has little debt.
A strong balance sheet helped the firm survive the crisis.
Accountants prepare the balance sheet at the end of the year.
Investors were worried about the bank's balance sheet.

meaning: The total value of sales a company makes in one year.
usage: British English; American English often uses “annual revenue”. Pattern: an annual turnover of £X.
examples: The company has an annual turnover of £10 million.
Small businesses with an annual turnover below the threshold don't pay VAT.
Annual turnover rose by 15 per cent.
The firm's annual turnover doubled in five years.

meaning: A twelve-month period used for financial reporting and taxes, which may not match the calendar year.
usage: British English often uses “financial year”. Pattern: in the fiscal year 2024–25.
examples: The company's fiscal year ends in March.
Profits rose in the last fiscal year.
The budget for the next fiscal year has been approved.
Sales were strong in the first half of the fiscal year.

meaning: A decrease in economic or business activity.
usage: Collocations: an economic/sharp/global downturn; a downturn in sales/the market. Opposite: an upturn.
examples: Many companies cut jobs during the economic downturn.
There has been a downturn in the housing market.
The industry is recovering from a sharp downturn.
A downturn in tourism hurt local businesses.

meaning: A period when economic activity declines significantly and unemployment rises.
usage: Verbs: go into/enter/come out of/emerge from a recession. Also: a global/deep recession.
examples: The country is facing an economic recession.
Unemployment rose sharply during the economic recession.
Economists predict an economic recession next year.
Small businesses suffered most in the economic recession.

meaning: An economy that is growing quickly and successfully.
usage: Also: a booming industry/market/town. The noun “boom” means rapid growth (an economic boom).
examples: Vietnam has a booming economy.
A booming economy creates more jobs.
The city's booming economy has attracted many workers.
House prices rise in a booming economy.

meaning: An increase in the production of goods and services in an economy over time.
usage: Adjectives: rapid/slow/steady/sustainable economic growth. Verbs: boost/stimulate/slow economic growth.
examples: The country has experienced rapid economic growth.
Investment in education boosts economic growth.
Economic growth slowed in the second quarter.
Is economic growth compatible with protecting the environment?

meaning: A plan designed to help a company, economy, or person return to a normal or healthy state.
usage: Verbs: draw up/announce/implement a recovery plan. Also: an economic/business recovery plan.
examples: The government announced an economic recovery plan.
The company drew up a recovery plan after heavy losses.
The recovery plan includes job cuts and new investment.
A good recovery plan helps businesses survive a crisis.

meaning: The purchase of a company against the wishes of its managers.
usage: Verbs: launch/fight off/resist a hostile takeover. Opposite: a friendly takeover.
examples: The company fought off a hostile takeover bid.
A rival firm launched a hostile takeover.
Hostile takeovers often lead to job losses.
The board rejected the hostile takeover.

meaning: A business project in which two or more companies work together and share profits and risks.
usage: Verbs: form/set up/enter into a joint venture with someone.
examples: The two companies formed a joint venture to build electric cars.
Foreign firms often enter the market through a joint venture.
The joint venture was a great success.
They set up a joint venture in Vietnam.

meaning: A new business, especially one in technology, that is in its early stages.
usage: Also simply “a start-up” (American: startup). Verbs: launch/found/run a start-up company.
examples: She left her job to launch a start-up company.
Many start-up companies fail within five years.
The start-up company was bought by Google.
Investors are funding a start-up company that develops medical apps.

meaning: A company with few employees and limited sales.
usage: Common in policy: support/help small businesses; small business owners. Often abbreviated SMEs (small and medium-sized enterprises).
examples: She runs a small business selling handmade jewellery.
The government offers loans to small businesses.
Small businesses were hit hard by the pandemic.
Shopping locally supports small businesses.

meaning: A large company that operates in many countries.
usage: Also: a multinational company; simply “a multinational”. Often discussed in globalization debates.
examples: She works for a multinational corporation in Singapore.
Multinational corporations have enormous economic power.
Critics say multinational corporations avoid paying taxes.
The multinational corporation employs over 100,000 people.

meaning: A company owned and run by members of one family.
usage: Verbs: run/join/take over/inherit a family business.
examples: He joined the family business after university.
The restaurant has been a family business for three generations.
Running a family business can cause family arguments.
She took over the family business from her father.

meaning: A group of people elected to manage and make major decisions for a company.
usage: Often shortened to “the board”. Verbs: sit on/join/appoint a board of directors.
examples: The board of directors approved the merger.
She was appointed to the board of directors.
The board of directors meets four times a year.
The CEO reports to the board of directors.

meaning: A manager at a high level in an organization.
usage: Also: senior management/staff/executive. Opposite: junior.
examples: She was promoted to senior manager last year.
Senior managers are responsible for strategic decisions.
The complaint was passed to a senior manager.
Several senior managers left the company.

meaning: The managers in an organization who are below senior management and above junior staff.
usage: Uncountable. Related: a middle manager. Often discussed in company restructuring.
examples: The company cut several jobs in middle management.
She's been in middle management for ten years.
Middle management often feels pressure from above and below.
Flat structures have fewer layers of middle management.

meaning: The person directly responsible for supervising an employee.
usage: Mainly British English. Pattern: talk to/report to your line manager.
examples: Speak to your line manager about holiday requests.
My line manager gives me feedback every week.
She reports directly to her line manager.
A good line manager supports staff development.
