meaning: To be responsible to someone and accept instructions from them at work.
usage: Pattern: report (directly) to someone. Also, report to a place means to go there officially.
examples: I report directly to the marketing director.
Who will the new manager report to?
All team leaders report to the head of operations.
New staff should report to reception on their first day.

meaning: The system in an organization by which instructions are passed from one level to the next.
usage: Also: follow/go through the chain of command. Common in military and corporate contexts.
examples: Complaints should go through the chain of command.
The army has a strict chain of command.
A clear chain of command avoids confusion.
Decisions were delayed because the chain of command was unclear.

meaning: An organizational structure with few levels of management between staff and leaders.
usage: Also: a flat structure/organization. Opposite: a rigid/strict hierarchy.
examples: Start-ups often have a flat hierarchy.
A flat hierarchy can speed up decision-making.
The company moved to a flat hierarchy last year.
In a flat hierarchy, junior staff talk directly to the CEO.

meaning: The shared values, beliefs, and behaviour within a company.
usage: Also: company/organizational/workplace culture. Adjectives: a positive/toxic/strong corporate culture.
examples: The company has a relaxed corporate culture.
Corporate culture affects employee happiness.
The new CEO wants to change the corporate culture.
A toxic corporate culture drives talented people away.

meaning: An official rule or plan of action followed by a company.
usage: Common phrases: “It's company policy to…”; against company policy. Also: a policy on something.
examples: It's company policy not to give refunds without a receipt.
Smoking indoors is against company policy.
The company policy on remote working has changed.
All staff must follow company policy.

meaning: To obey official rules.
usage: Also: comply with the law/rules/standards. Noun: compliance. Opposite: breach regulations.
examples: All products must comply with safety regulations.
Companies that fail to comply with regulations face fines.
The factory was closed for failing to comply with regulations.
We work hard to comply with environmental regulations.

meaning: The rules and practices that protect people from harm at work or in public places.
usage: Often used before nouns: health and safety regulations/training/officer. Sometimes used humorously for overcautious rules.
examples: All staff must complete health and safety training.
The factory was fined for breaking health and safety rules.
Health and safety is everyone's responsibility.
The event was cancelled for health and safety reasons.

meaning: A set of rules about how people in an organization should behave.
usage: Verbs: follow/breach/adopt a code of conduct. Similar: code of practice/ethics.
examples: All employees must follow the company's code of conduct.
He was dismissed for breaching the code of conduct.
The school has a strict code of conduct.
The code of conduct bans accepting gifts from clients.

meaning: Moral principles that guide how companies and people in business should behave.
usage: Uncountable (treated as singular or plural). Common as a university subject.
examples: The scandal raised serious questions about business ethics.
She teaches business ethics at the university.
Good business ethics build customer trust.
Business ethics should guide every decision.

meaning: A situation in which someone's personal interests could influence their professional decisions unfairly.
usage: Verbs: declare/avoid/have a conflict of interest. Plural: conflicts of interest.
examples: The judge stepped down because of a conflict of interest.
Employees must declare any conflict of interest.
Hiring your own brother creates a conflict of interest.
There's a clear conflict of interest here.

meaning: A company's commitment to act in ways that benefit society and the environment.
usage: Often abbreviated to CSR. Common in business studies and company reports.
examples: The company publishes a corporate social responsibility report every year.
Corporate social responsibility includes supporting local communities.
Critics say some corporate social responsibility is just marketing.
Investors increasingly care about corporate social responsibility.

meaning: A company that operates without harming the environment or society and can last long-term.
usage: Also: sustainable growth/practices/development. Verbs: build/run a sustainable business.
examples: She wants to build a sustainable business that reduces plastic waste.
Consumers increasingly support sustainable businesses.
Running a sustainable business can also be profitable.
The course teaches how to create a sustainable business.

meaning: The relationship between how much of a product is available and how much people want it, which affects price.
usage: Fixed order: supply and demand (not “demand and supply”). Also: the law of supply and demand.
examples: Prices are determined by supply and demand.
The law of supply and demand explains rising house prices.
When supply and demand are balanced, prices stay stable.
Students learn about supply and demand in economics.

meaning: The network of companies and processes involved in producing and delivering a product.
usage: Collocations: global/disrupted supply chains; supply chain management/problems/disruption.
examples: The pandemic disrupted global supply chains.
Companies are checking their supply chains for forced labour.
A short supply chain reduces delivery times.
Problems in the supply chain caused shortages.

meaning: To make a process simpler and more efficient.
usage: Also: streamline operations/procedures/the system. Adjective: streamlined.
examples: The new software streamlined the ordering process.
We need to streamline the process for approving expenses.
Automation helps streamline processes.
They streamlined the hiring process to reduce delays.

meaning: To make work or a system produce better results with less time, money, or effort.
usage: Also: increase/boost efficiency; energy efficiency. Adjective: efficient.
examples: The new system has improved efficiency in the warehouse.
Technology can improve efficiency in hospitals.
We're looking for ways to improve efficiency.
Training staff improved efficiency by 20 per cent.

meaning: To increase the amount of work produced.
usage: Also: increase/improve/raise productivity. Opposite: reduce/hurt productivity.
examples: Short breaks can boost productivity.
The company introduced flexible hours to boost productivity.
Does working from home boost productivity?
New machinery boosted productivity on the farm.

meaning: A job that takes a lot of time to do.
usage: Also: a time-consuming process/job. Hyphenated before a noun.
examples: Entering data manually is a time-consuming task.
Writing reports is a time-consuming task.
AI can automate many time-consuming tasks.
Checking every invoice was a time-consuming task.

meaning: To do something badly or cheaply, often ignoring rules, to save time or money.
usage: It is informal and critical. Common in discussions of safety and quality.
examples: The builders cut corners and the roof leaked.
Don't cut corners on safety.
Companies that cut corners often face problems later.
We can't afford to cut corners on this project.

meaning: A fast and easy solution that does not solve the problem permanently.
usage: Often negative: “There's no quick fix.” Opposite: a long-term solution.
examples: There's no quick fix for the housing crisis.
Cutting prices is just a quick fix.
We need a proper solution, not a quick fix.
Diet pills are a dangerous quick fix.

meaning: A way of solving a problem that will work for a long time.
usage: Verbs: find/seek/provide a long-term solution. Opposite: a short-term fix/quick fix.
examples: We need a long-term solution to traffic congestion.
Building more homes is the only long-term solution.
The government has yet to find a long-term solution.
This is a temporary measure, not a long-term solution.

meaning: A choice that is practical and likely to succeed.
usage: Also: a viable alternative/solution/plan. Often negative: “not a viable option”.
examples: Renting is a viable option for many young people.
Closing the factory is not a viable option.
Electric cars are now a viable option for most drivers.
We need to consider every viable option.

meaning: A plan that is possible and practical to carry out.
usage: Also: a feasible option/solution/idea. Related: a feasibility study.
examples: We need a feasible plan, not wishful thinking.
Is this a feasible plan given our budget?
The engineers came up with a feasible plan.
Without funding, the project is not a feasible plan.

meaning: To consider the advantages and disadvantages of different choices before deciding.
usage: British English often uses “weigh up”; American English “weigh”. Also: weigh up the pros and cons.
examples: Take time to weigh up the options before you decide.
She weighed up the options and chose the cheaper flight.
We need to weigh up the options carefully.
After weighing up the options, he accepted the offer.

meaning: A risk taken after carefully considering the likely results.
usage: Verbs: take a calculated risk. It suggests sensible, informed risk-taking.
examples: Investing in the new market was a calculated risk.
Starting a business always involves a calculated risk.
She took a calculated risk and it paid off.
The coach took a calculated risk by changing tactics.

meaning: To do something even though it might have bad results.
usage: Also: take risks; run a risk. Adjectives: a big/huge/calculated risk.
examples: Successful entrepreneurs are willing to take risks.
I don't want to take a risk with my savings.
She took a big risk by moving abroad.
Sometimes you have to take a risk to succeed.

meaning: To reduce the chance or impact of something bad happening.
usage: Also: reduce/minimize/manage risks. Common in project management and finance. Noun: risk mitigation.
examples: We need a plan to mitigate risks before the launch.
Insurance helps mitigate financial risks.
Good training can mitigate the risks of accidents.
The report suggests ways to mitigate risks.

meaning: A careful examination of possible dangers in an activity and how to reduce them.
usage: Verbs: carry out/conduct/do a risk assessment. Required in many workplaces and schools.
examples: Teachers must carry out a risk assessment before a school trip.
The company conducted a risk assessment of the new site.
A risk assessment identified several hazards.
Every event needs a proper risk assessment.

meaning: The worst possible situation that could happen.
usage: Common phrase: in the worst-case scenario. Opposite: a best-case scenario.
examples: In the worst-case scenario, we'll lose the contract.
Plan for the worst-case scenario.
The worst-case scenario is a delay of six months.
Experts described a worst-case scenario for sea levels.

meaning: A plan to be used if something goes wrong.
usage: Verbs: have/draw up/put in place a contingency plan. Similar: a backup plan, plan B.
examples: We have a contingency plan in case of bad weather.
Every business needs a contingency plan.
The hospital put a contingency plan in place.
Our contingency plan worked perfectly.

meaning: An alternative plan to use if the original plan fails.
usage: Informal synonym: plan B. Also: have/need a backup plan.
examples: Always have a backup plan.
Our backup plan was to hold the event indoors.
If the flight is cancelled, what's our backup plan?
She had a backup plan in case she didn't get into university.

meaning: The process of dealing with a sudden emergency or serious problem in an organization.
usage: Uncountable. Related: a crisis management team/plan.
examples: The company's crisis management was widely praised.
She specializes in crisis management.
Good crisis management can protect a brand's reputation.
The government was criticized for poor crisis management.

meaning: Actions taken to limit the harm caused by a mistake or bad event, especially to reputation.
usage: British English also “damage limitation”. Common in politics and PR: “in damage control mode”.
examples: After the scandal, the company went into damage control.
The press release was an attempt at damage control.
The minister spent the week doing damage control.
Quick apologies are an important part of damage control.

meaning: A situation, often a mistake or difficulty, from which you can learn something.
usage: Often used positively to reframe failure: “Treat every mistake as a learning opportunity.”
examples: Every mistake is a learning opportunity.
The failed project was a valuable learning opportunity.
Internships offer great learning opportunities.
Treat criticism as a learning opportunity.

meaning: A situation in which competing companies keep lowering their prices to win customers.
usage: Verbs: start/trigger/be locked in a price war. It benefits consumers but can hurt profits.
examples: The supermarkets are engaged in a price war.
A price war between airlines has lowered fares.
Small shops can't survive a price war.
The new competitor started a price war.

meaning: A sudden large increase in price.
usage: Informal, common in news. Also: a price increase/rise. Verb: hike prices.
examples: Customers are angry about the latest price hike.
The energy company announced a 20 per cent price hike.
Another price hike could reduce demand.
Students protested against the tuition price hike.

meaning: A product sold at a lower price than usual for a limited time.
usage: Patterns: on special offer; a special offer on something. Also: a limited-time offer.
examples: These shoes are on special offer this week.
The supermarket has a special offer on coffee.
Sign up now to take advantage of our special offer.
The special offer ends on Sunday.

meaning: A large order of goods, usually at a lower price per item.
usage: Related: buy in bulk; bulk discount/purchase.
examples: We offer discounts on bulk orders.
The school placed a bulk order for textbooks.
Bulk orders are delivered within two weeks.
A bulk order of 1,000 units qualifies for free delivery.

meaning: To ask a company to supply goods.
usage: Pattern: place an order for something with someone. Related: process/cancel/track an order.
examples: I placed an order for a new laptop online.
You can place an order by phone or online.
The restaurant placed an order with a local farm.
Orders placed before noon are delivered the next day.

meaning: To deal with an order so that the goods can be sent.
usage: Related: order processing; your order is being processed.
examples: Your order is being processed.
It takes two days to process an order.
The warehouse processes thousands of orders a day.
We'll process your order as soon as payment is received.

meaning: Not available because all items have been sold.
usage: Opposite: in stock. Also: sold out; go out of stock.
examples: Sorry, that size is out of stock.
The new phone went out of stock within hours.
The item is temporarily out of stock.
Popular toys are often out of stock before Christmas.

meaning: A company's rules about when customers can get their money back.
usage: Also: a returns policy; a no-refund policy.
examples: Check the refund policy before you buy.
The shop has a generous refund policy.
Their refund policy allows returns within 30 days.
The airline changed its refund policy during the pandemic.

meaning: To give a customer their money back.
usage: Also: give/provide a refund; get/receive/claim a refund (customer). Formal business language.
examples: The airline issued a refund for the cancelled flight.
We will issue a refund within five working days.
The shop refused to issue a refund without a receipt.
Once we receive the item, we'll issue a full refund.

meaning: To pay the amount shown on a bill for goods or services.
usage: Also: send/issue/raise an invoice (supplier). Irregular: paid. Pattern: pay an invoice within 30 days.
examples: Please pay the invoice within 30 days.
The client still hasn't paid our invoice.
We pay invoices at the end of each month.
Invoices must be paid by bank transfer.

meaning: A payment that is still owed and has not yet been made.
usage: “Outstanding” here means unpaid, not excellent. Also: an outstanding debt/balance/invoice.
examples: We have several outstanding payments from clients.
Please settle the outstanding payment as soon as possible.
Your account will be suspended until the outstanding payment is made.
The company chased up all outstanding payments.

meaning: A payment made after the date it was due.
usage: Related: a late payment fee/charge; late payments hurt small businesses.
examples: There's a fee for late payment.
Late payments cause cash flow problems for suppliers.
The bank charged me for a late payment.
Repeated late payments can damage your credit rating.

meaning: An arrangement to pay a debt or purchase in smaller amounts over time.
usage: Verbs: set up/agree/offer a payment plan. Similar: an instalment plan.
examples: The university offers a payment plan for tuition fees.
We agreed a payment plan with the customer.
You can buy the sofa on a twelve-month payment plan.
Contact us if you need to set up a payment plan.

meaning: A journey made for work purposes.
usage: Verbs: go on/be on/take a business trip. Also: travel on business.
examples: She's away on a business trip to Tokyo.
He goes on business trips almost every month.
The company pays for meals on business trips.
I combined my business trip with a short holiday.

meaning: A gathering where people meet to make professional contacts.
usage: Verbs: attend/go to/host a networking event. Related verb: network (with someone).
examples: I met my business partner at a networking event.
The university hosts networking events for graduates.
Bring business cards to the networking event.
Networking events can feel awkward at first.

meaning: To develop a group of professional contacts who can help you.
usage: Also: build/expand/grow your network; a professional network.
examples: LinkedIn helps you build a professional network.
It takes years to build a strong network.
She built a network of contacts across Asia.
Internships are a great way to build a network.

meaning: To meet people who may be useful professionally; also, to see links between ideas.
usage: Both senses are common. Also: make contacts.
examples: Conferences are a good place to make connections.
She made valuable connections during her internship.
Good students make connections between different topics.
Volunteering helped him make connections in the industry.

meaning: A large event where companies show and sell their products to other businesses.
usage: Also: a trade show/exhibition. Verbs: attend/exhibit at/organize a trade fair.
examples: We exhibited our products at a trade fair in Frankfurt.
The trade fair attracted thousands of buyers.
She met new suppliers at the trade fair.
The company launches its new products at the annual trade fair.

meaning: The event or process of introducing a new product to the market.
usage: Verbs: plan/hold/organize a product launch. Related verb: launch a product.
examples: The product launch is scheduled for September.
Hundreds of journalists attended the product launch.
The product launch was delayed by supply problems.
A successful product launch needs good marketing.

meaning: An official statement given to journalists.
usage: Verbs: issue/send out/publish a press release.
examples: The company issued a press release announcing the merger.
According to the press release, sales rose by 10 per cent.
We'll send out a press release tomorrow.
The press release was picked up by several newspapers.

meaning: How familiar people are with a brand.
usage: Uncountable. Verbs: raise/increase/build brand awareness.
examples: Social media helps raise brand awareness.
The campaign increased brand awareness among young people.
Sponsoring events builds brand awareness.
Brand awareness is low in rural areas.

meaning: The tendency of customers to keep buying the same brand.
usage: Uncountable. Verbs: build/create/increase brand loyalty.
examples: Apple has strong brand loyalty.
Loyalty programmes help build brand loyalty.
Young consumers show less brand loyalty than older ones.
Good customer service increases brand loyalty.

meaning: A planned series of activities to promote a product or service.
usage: Verbs: launch/run/plan a marketing campaign. Also: an advertising campaign.
examples: The company launched a marketing campaign on TikTok.
The marketing campaign boosted sales by 30 per cent.
She manages marketing campaigns for a fashion brand.
The marketing campaign targeted university students.

meaning: Promoting products or services using social media platforms.
usage: Uncountable. Related: digital marketing; a social media strategy/campaign.
examples: Social media marketing is essential for small businesses.
She works in social media marketing.
The brand spends most of its budget on social media marketing.
Social media marketing helps reach younger customers.

meaning: Information passed from person to person by talking, especially recommendations.
usage: Pattern: by/through word of mouth; word-of-mouth marketing/recommendations.
examples: The restaurant grew through word of mouth.
Most of our customers find us by word of mouth.
Word of mouth is the most powerful form of advertising.
The film's success was driven by word of mouth.

meaning: The particular group of people that a product, advert, or message is aimed at.
usage: Verbs: reach/identify/appeal to a target audience. Also used in writing and media.
examples: Our target audience is people aged 18 to 25.
The advert failed to reach its target audience.
Know your target audience before you write.
The film's target audience is teenagers.

meaning: A feature that makes a product different from and better than competitors.
usage: Often abbreviated to USP. American English also “unique selling proposition”.
examples: The phone's unique selling point is its battery life.
Every business needs a unique selling point.
Free delivery is our unique selling point.
What's the unique selling point of your product?

meaning: The company or product with the largest share of a market.
usage: Pattern: a market leader in something. Also: become/remain the market leader.
examples: The company is a market leader in electric bikes.
Google remains the market leader in online search.
They became the market leader within five years.
Challenging the market leader is difficult.

meaning: A very important person, company, or country in an activity or industry.
usage: Pattern: a key player in something. Also used in sport and politics.
examples: China is a key player in the global economy.
She was a key player in the negotiations.
The company has become a key player in renewable energy.
Several key players left the industry last year.

meaning: The price of one share of a company on the stock market.
usage: Collocations: the share price rose/fell/plunged/soared. American English: stock price.
examples: The company's share price fell after the scandal.
The share price has doubled this year.
Investors watched the share price closely.
Good results pushed up the share price.

meaning: The system or place where shares in companies are bought and sold.
usage: Collocations: invest in/play the stock market; a stock market crash/index.
examples: He lost a lot of money on the stock market.
The stock market fell sharply this morning.
Many young people invest in the stock market through apps.
The stock market crash of 1929 led to the Great Depression.

meaning: To put money, time, or effort into something to get a benefit later.
usage: Patterns: invest money in something; invest time/effort in (doing) something. Noun: investment.
examples: The company invested heavily in new technology.
It's worth investing in a good mattress.
Governments should invest in education.
She invested her savings in property.

meaning: An investment that is safe and likely to bring benefits.
usage: “Sound” here means reliable and sensible. Also: a good/wise/risky investment.
examples: Property is usually considered a sound investment.
Education is a sound investment in your future.
Was buying the company a sound investment?
Gold is seen as a sound investment in uncertain times.

meaning: A person or company with whom you share ownership or work on a business.
usage: Also: a trading partner. Verbs: find/look for a business partner.
examples: She started the company with a business partner.
Choose your business partner carefully.
Japan is an important business partner for Vietnam.
He fell out with his business partner.

meaning: A presentation or speech intended to persuade someone to buy something.
usage: Verbs: make/give/deliver a sales pitch. Related: pitch a product.
examples: He gave a convincing sales pitch to the client.
I'm tired of hearing the same sales pitch.
Keep your sales pitch short and clear.
Her sales pitch convinced the client to sign immediately.

meaning: An amount of sales that a person or company aims to achieve.
usage: Verbs: set/meet/hit/exceed/miss a sales target.
examples: The team exceeded its sales target this quarter.
Each salesperson has a monthly sales target.
We missed our sales target by five per cent.
Sales targets can create a lot of pressure.

meaning: An aggressive way of persuading someone to buy something; also, something difficult to persuade people to accept.
usage: Verbs: give someone the hard sell. Opposite: a soft sell. Figuratively: “The plan will be a hard sell to voters.”
examples: The salesman gave us the hard sell.
I hate it when shops use the hard sell.
Raising taxes is always a hard sell.
The new rules will be a hard sell to staff.

meaning: An estimate of how much a company will sell in a future period.
usage: Verbs: prepare/make/revise a sales forecast.
examples: The sales forecast for next year looks positive.
We revised our sales forecast after the recession.
Accurate sales forecasts help with planning.
The sales forecast was too optimistic.

meaning: To prepare and write a formal contract.
usage: Also: draw up a plan/list/agreement. Irregular: drew, drawn.
examples: The lawyer drew up a contract for the sale.
We need to draw up a contract before work begins.
The contract was drawn up by our legal team.
Can you draw up a contract for the new client?

meaning: The rules and details of an agreement or service.
usage: Fixed order. Often abbreviated to T&Cs. Verbs: read/accept/agree to the terms and conditions.
examples: Few people read the terms and conditions before clicking “accept”.
The terms and conditions say refunds are not allowed.
Please agree to the terms and conditions to continue.
The company changed its terms and conditions last month.

meaning: The detailed, often less obvious parts of a contract or agreement.
usage: British English also “the small print”. Common advice: “Always read the fine print.”
examples: Always read the fine print before signing.
The fine print said there was a cancellation fee.
Hidden costs were buried in the fine print.
I didn't read the fine print and regretted it.

meaning: An agreement made by speaking rather than in writing.
usage: Also: an oral agreement. Contrast: a written agreement. Verbal agreements can be hard to prove.
examples: We had only a verbal agreement, so nothing was in writing.
A verbal agreement can be legally binding in some cases.
They reached a verbal agreement over the phone.
Always follow up a verbal agreement with an email.

meaning: An agreement that must legally be followed.
usage: Also: legally binding; a binding contract/decision. Opposite: a non-binding agreement.
examples: Once signed, this is a binding agreement.
The two companies entered into a binding agreement.
Is the deal a legally binding agreement?
The countries failed to reach a binding agreement on emissions.

meaning: To agree on a solution in which each side gives up something.
usage: Also: come to/agree on a compromise. Pattern: reach a compromise on/over something.
examples: After long talks, they reached a compromise on pay.
We reached a compromise: half the meetings will be online.
Both parties are willing to reach a compromise.
It's hard to reach a compromise when neither side will listen.

meaning: To accept some of another person's demands so that you can agree; to compromise.
usage: Pattern: meet someone halfway. Informal and common in negotiation.
examples: If you lower the price a little, I'll meet you halfway.
Both sides need to meet halfway.
The landlord agreed to meet us halfway on the rent.
Let's meet halfway and split the cost.

meaning: A situation in which everyone involved benefits.
usage: Also simply “a win-win”. Opposite: a lose-lose situation.
examples: Flexible hours are a win-win situation for staff and employers.
Recycling the materials creates a win-win situation.
Negotiators aim for a win-win situation.
Lower prices and higher sales: it's a win-win situation.

meaning: Something used to gain an advantage in a negotiation.
usage: Verbs: use something as a bargaining chip. Common in politics and trade talks.
examples: The union used the threat of a strike as a bargaining chip.
Natural resources are a powerful bargaining chip.
Don't use your children as a bargaining chip.
A competing job offer is a useful bargaining chip in salary talks.

meaning: A factor that would cause someone to reject an agreement.
usage: Also written “dealbreaker”. Used in business and relationships.
examples: The long commute was a deal breaker for me.
For many buyers, the high price is a deal breaker.
Is smoking a deal breaker for you?
The lack of parking turned out to be a deal breaker.

meaning: An issue that prevents people from reaching an agreement.
usage: Often “the main/major sticking point”. Common in news about negotiations.
examples: Pay remains the main sticking point in the talks.
The deadline was a sticking point for both sides.
Fishing rights became a major sticking point.
Once the sticking point was resolved, the deal was signed.

meaning: Opinions or interests that two or more people share, despite other differences.
usage: Verbs: find/look for/seek/share common ground. Uncountable.
examples: The two parties have little common ground.
Despite their differences, they share some common ground.
Negotiations begin by identifying common ground.
Music gave them common ground to start a friendship.

meaning: To discover shared opinions or interests that allow agreement.
usage: Pattern: find common ground with someone/on something.
examples: The two sides struggled to find common ground.
Good negotiators find common ground quickly.
We found common ground on most issues.
It's important to find common ground with your colleagues.

meaning: Having the same understanding or agreement about something.
usage: Informal. Common in meetings: “Let's make sure we're all on the same page.”
examples: Let's make sure we're all on the same page before we start.
The managers aren't on the same page about the budget.
A quick meeting helped get everyone on the same page.
Are we on the same page about the deadline?

meaning: To think creatively and in an original way.
usage: Informal and sometimes considered a cliché. Similar: think creatively.
examples: We need to think outside the box to solve this problem.
The company encourages staff to think outside the box.
She's great at thinking outside the box.
Thinking outside the box led to a brilliant idea.

meaning: A meeting in which people suggest many ideas quickly to solve a problem.
usage: Verbs: hold/have/run a brainstorming session. Verb: brainstorm ideas.
examples: We held a brainstorming session to plan the campaign.
The best ideas came from a brainstorming session.
Let's have a quick brainstorming session.
In a brainstorming session, no idea is a bad idea.

meaning: To think of new ideas.
usage: Also: come up with a plan/solution/name/excuse. Irregular: came.
examples: We need to come up with ideas for the new advert.
She came up with ideas nobody else had thought of.
It's hard to come up with ideas when you're tired.
The team came up with ideas to reduce waste.

meaning: To present an idea to someone in order to persuade them to accept it.
usage: Pattern: pitch an idea to someone. Related: make a pitch; an elevator pitch.
examples: She pitched an idea for a new app to investors.
I'll pitch the idea to my manager tomorrow.
He pitched an idea for a TV show to the network.
Practise before you pitch an idea to clients.

meaning: To tell someone about an idea to get their opinion.
usage: Pattern: run something by someone. Informal: “Can I run something by you?”
examples: Can I run an idea by you?
I ran the idea by my boss, and she liked it.
Let me run this idea by the team first.
She ran her idea by a few friends before starting the business.

meaning: To receive permission to go ahead with something.
usage: Also: give something the green light. Similar: get the go-ahead.
examples: The project got the green light from the board.
We're still waiting to get the green light.
The film finally got the green light after years of delays.
The new stadium finally got the green light from the council.

meaning: To give permission for something to start.
usage: Pattern: give someone/something the go-ahead. Also: get/receive the go-ahead.
examples: The manager gave the go-ahead for the new website.
The government gave the go-ahead to build the airport.
Once the client gives the go-ahead, we'll start.
Doctors gave her the go-ahead to return to work.

meaning: To delay something until a later time; also, to make a phone caller wait.
usage: Pattern: put something on hold. Also: be on hold.
examples: The project has been put on hold due to lack of funding.
She put her studies on hold to look after her mother.
I was put on hold for twenty minutes.
All hiring has been put on hold.

meaning: Being planned or developed and likely to happen soon.
usage: Common phrase: “We have several projects in the pipeline.”
examples: The company has several new products in the pipeline.
More changes are in the pipeline.
A pay rise is in the pipeline.
There's a sequel in the pipeline.

meaning: The most important thing to deal with.
usage: Also: a high/low priority; make something a top priority.
examples: Customer safety is our top priority.
The government has made education a top priority.
Finishing the report is my top priority today.
Reducing costs is a top priority for the new CEO.

meaning: To decide which things are most important and should be done first.
usage: Also: get your priorities right/straight. Related verb: prioritize.
examples: Good managers know how to set priorities.
Set priorities at the start of each week.
The government needs to set clear priorities.
Setting priorities helps reduce stress.

meaning: Something that completely changes a situation or the way things are done.
usage: Informal. Also written “game-changer”. Common in tech and business writing.
examples: Smartphones were a game changer for the travel industry.
This new battery could be a game changer.
Remote work has been a game changer for parents.
The new coach proved to be a game changer.

meaning: A situation in which everyone has the same chances of success.
usage: Verbs: create/ensure a level playing field. Common in discussions of fairness and competition.
examples: The new rules create a level playing field for small businesses.
Students from poor families don't compete on a level playing field.
We want a level playing field for all suppliers.
Regulators aim to ensure a level playing field.

meaning: Very fierce competition in which people or companies will do anything to win.
usage: Also: a cut-throat industry/business/market. Hyphenated.
examples: The airline industry faces cut-throat competition.
Cut-throat competition has driven prices down.
Small shops can't survive such cut-throat competition.
Fashion is known for its cut-throat competition.

meaning: Very strong competition.
usage: Also: intense/stiff/tough competition. Pattern: fierce competition for/between/from.
examples: There's fierce competition for places at top universities.
The company faces fierce competition from online retailers.
Fierce competition keeps prices low.
There was fierce competition between the two candidates.

meaning: To continue to be more successful than competitors.
usage: Also: keep ahead of/get ahead of the competition.
examples: Companies must innovate to stay ahead of the competition.
Investing in staff helps us stay ahead of the competition.
It's hard to stay ahead of the competition in tech.
Good customer service helped them stay ahead of the competition.

meaning: To choose what to do after thinking about it.
usage: Also: take a decision (British, formal); a difficult/big/quick decision. Avoid “do a decision”.
examples: I need to make a decision by Friday.
It was the hardest decision I've ever made.
Don't make a decision when you're angry.
The decision was made after long discussions.

meaning: To try hard to do something.
usage: Pattern: make an effort to do something. Also: make a real/special/conscious effort.
examples: I'm making an effort to eat more vegetables.
She made a real effort to be friendly.
You need to make more effort in class.
Thanks for making the effort to come.

meaning: To do something wrong.
usage: Also: make an error. Avoid “do a mistake”. Adjectives: a big/common/silly/costly mistake.
examples: Everyone makes mistakes.
I made a mistake in the calculation.
Don't worry about making mistakes when you speak.
We made a big mistake when we hired him.

meaning: To improve or develop over time.
usage: Uncountable: “make good/great/slow progress” (not “a progress”).
examples: She's making good progress with her English.
We've made a lot of progress on the project.
The patient is making slow but steady progress.
Are you making any progress?

meaning: To give a reason, often untrue, to explain why you did or didn't do something.
usage: Also: make excuses (for someone). Related: a good/poor/lame excuse.
examples: He always makes an excuse to leave early.
Stop making excuses and do your homework.
She made an excuse about being ill.
Don't make excuses for his bad behaviour.

meaning: To complain or get upset about something, usually more than is necessary.
usage: Pattern: make a fuss about/over something. “Make a fuss of someone” means to give them a lot of attention.
examples: Don't make a fuss about such a small thing.
She made a fuss when her order was wrong.
My grandparents always make a fuss of me when I visit.
He hates people making a fuss over his birthday.

meaning: To have just enough money to pay for the things you need.
usage: Often used with difficulty: struggle to/can barely make ends meet.
examples: Many families are struggling to make ends meet.
She works two jobs to make ends meet.
With rising prices, it's hard to make ends meet.
As a student, I could barely make ends meet.

meaning: To earn enough money to support yourself.
usage: Patterns: make a living from/as/by doing something. Also: earn a living.
examples: He makes a living as a freelance photographer.
It's difficult to make a living from writing.
Most people in the village make a living by fishing.
She makes a good living selling cakes online.

meaning: To form friendships with people.
usage: Pattern: make friends with someone. Also: make new friends.
examples: It's easy to make friends at university.
She made friends with her new neighbours.
Moving abroad helped me make friends from all over the world.
Some children find it hard to make friends.

meaning: To have an effect, especially a good one.
usage: Also: make a big/real/huge difference; make no difference (have no effect).
examples: Small changes can make a big difference.
Teachers make a real difference in children's lives.
It makes no difference to me where we eat.
Volunteering is a great way to make a difference.

meaning: To be easy to understand or reasonable.
usage: Patterns: it makes sense to do something; make sense of something (understand it).
examples: Your explanation makes sense.
It makes sense to book early.
I couldn't make sense of the instructions.
Does this sentence make sense?

meaning: To use an opportunity or situation as well as possible.
usage: Typical objects: an opportunity, your time, the weather, the situation.
examples: Make the most of your time at university.
We made the most of the sunny weather.
She made the most of every opportunity.
Let's make the most of our last day here.

meaning: To arrange a time to see someone, such as a doctor.
usage: Pattern: make an appointment with someone/to do something. Also: book an appointment.
examples: I need to make an appointment with the dentist.
You can make an appointment online.
She made an appointment to see a lawyer.
Please make an appointment before visiting the office.

meaning: To arrange to have a table, room, or seat kept for you.
usage: Also: book a table/room. Pattern: make a reservation for two at 8 p.m.
examples: I've made a reservation at an Italian restaurant.
Can I make a reservation for four people?
We made a reservation at the hotel months ago.
You don't need to make a reservation for lunch.

meaning: To say formally that you are not satisfied with something.
usage: Pattern: make a complaint about something/to someone. Also: file/lodge a complaint.
examples: I'd like to make a complaint about the service.
She made a complaint to the manager.
Several guests made complaints about the noise.
You can make a complaint online.

meaning: To have an effect on how people think about you.
usage: Adjectives: a good/great/bad/lasting impression. Pattern: make an impression on someone.
examples: She made a great impression at the interview.
You only have one chance to make a first impression.
His speech made a strong impression on the audience.
I want to make a good impression on my new boss.

meaning: To do the regular jobs of cleaning and tidying a home.
usage: “Housework” is uncountable. Also: do household chores. Avoid “make the housework”.
examples: We take turns to do the housework.
I do the housework on Saturday mornings.
He never does the housework without being asked.
Doing the housework can be good exercise.

meaning: To wash the plates, cups, and pans after a meal.
usage: Also: do the washing-up (British); wash the dishes.
examples: It's your turn to do the dishes.
I'll cook if you do the dishes.
He did the dishes before going to bed.
We have a dishwasher, so nobody has to do the dishes.

meaning: To try as hard as you can.
usage: Also: try your best. Commonly used to encourage: “Just do your best.”
examples: Don't worry about the result; just do your best.
I did my best, but I still failed.
She always does her best at work.
We'll do our best to help you.

meaning: To help someone by doing something for them.
usage: American spelling: favor. Common request: “Could you do me a favour?” Also: ask someone a favour.
examples: Could you do me a favour and feed my cat?
He did me a big favour by lending me his car.
I owe you one for doing me that favour.
Do yourself a favour and get some sleep.

meaning: To complete schoolwork set for home; figuratively, to prepare carefully by researching.
usage: “Homework” is uncountable. Figurative: “Do your homework before buying a car.”
examples: Have you done your homework yet?
Do your homework before dinner.
Investors should do their homework before buying shares.
She clearly did her homework before the interview.

meaning: To buy food and household items, usually regularly.
usage: Also: go shopping (often for pleasure). “Do the shopping” suggests a routine task.
examples: I usually do the shopping on Sundays.
Who's doing the shopping this week?
We do the shopping online now.
She does the shopping for her elderly neighbour.

meaning: To cause more problems than benefits.
usage: Often a warning: “That will do more harm than good.”
examples: Too much exercise can do more harm than good.
Shouting at children often does more harm than good.
The new rules may do more harm than good.
Taking antibiotics unnecessarily does more harm than good.

meaning: To cause harm.
usage: Patterns: do damage to something; do (serious/lasting) damage. “Damage” is uncountable here.
examples: The storm did a lot of damage to the roof.
Smoking does serious damage to your lungs.
The scandal did lasting damage to his reputation.
Too much sun can do damage to your skin.

meaning: To stop working or doing something for a short time to rest.
usage: Also: have a break (British). Pattern: take a break from something.
examples: Let's take a break for ten minutes.
You should take a break from your screen every hour.
She took a break from work to travel.
I took a short break and then carried on.

meaning: To use a camera or phone to make a picture.
usage: Also: take a picture. Avoid “make a photo”. Pattern: take a photo of someone/something.
examples: Could you take a photo of us?
I took hundreds of photos on holiday.
You're not allowed to take photos in the museum.
She took a photo of the sunset.

meaning: To sit down.
usage: Polite phrase: “Please take a seat.” Also: have a seat.
examples: Please take a seat; the doctor will see you soon.
He took a seat at the back of the room.
Take a seat and make yourself comfortable.
She took a seat next to me on the bus.

meaning: To do something slowly and carefully, without hurrying.
usage: Often said to reassure someone: “Take your time.”
examples: Take your time; there's no rush.
She took her time choosing a dress.
Take your time and read the questions carefully.
He's taking his time replying to my email.

meaning: To use an opportunity; also, to use someone unfairly for your own benefit.
usage: Both meanings are common: take advantage of an offer (positive); take advantage of someone (negative).
examples: Take advantage of the free lessons while you can.
I took advantage of the sale to buy a new coat.
Don't let people take advantage of your kindness.
He took advantage of her trust.

meaning: To be involved in an activity with other people.
usage: Also: participate in (more formal). Pattern: take part in a competition/discussion/survey.
examples: Over 1,000 runners took part in the marathon.
All students are encouraged to take part in the debate.
Would you like to take part in our survey?
She took part in a protest against climate change.

meaning: To happen, especially as planned.
usage: It has no passive form (not “was taken place”). Pattern: take place in/at/on…
examples: The wedding will take place in June.
Where did the meeting take place?
The concert took place in the main square.
Big changes are taking place in the industry.

meaning: To look after someone or something; also, to deal with a task.
usage: Also: look after. “I'll take care of it” means I'll deal with it. “Take care!” is an informal goodbye.
examples: She takes care of her younger brother after school.
Don't worry about the bill; I'll take care of it.
Take care of yourself and get some rest.
Who will take care of the dog while we're away?

meaning: To relax and not work too hard; also, to stay calm.
usage: Informal. Often advice: “Take it easy for a few days.” Also used to calm someone: “Take it easy!”
examples: The doctor told me to take it easy for a week.
Take it easy this weekend; you've worked hard.
Take it easy! There's no need to shout.
We just took it easy on holiday.

meaning: To sleep for a short time during the day.
usage: Also: have a nap (British). A short nap is sometimes called a “power nap”.
examples: I usually take a nap after lunch.
The baby is taking a nap.
If you feel tired, take a nap for twenty minutes.
He took a nap on the sofa.

meaning: To do something risky because it might succeed.
usage: Patterns: take a chance on someone/something; take chances. Similar: take a risk.
examples: I decided to take a chance and apply for the job.
The company took a chance on an unknown designer.
Don't take chances with your health.
Sometimes you have to take a chance.

meaning: To feel upset or insulted by something someone says or does.
usage: American spelling: offense. Pattern: take offence at something. Also: no offence (meant).
examples: She took offence at his comment about her cooking.
I didn't mean to offend you; please don't take offence.
He takes offence too easily.
Many viewers took offence at the advert.

meaning: To become the leader in a race or competition; also, to take control of a situation.
usage: Pattern: take the lead in something/doing something.
examples: The team took the lead in the second half.
She took the lead in organizing the event.
Someone needs to take the lead on this project.
The runner took the lead with one lap to go.

meaning: To expect something to always be available or true, and so not appreciate it; to assume something without questioning it.
usage: Patterns: take someone/something for granted; take it for granted that…
examples: We often take clean water for granted.
She felt her husband took her for granted.
Don't take your health for granted.
I took it for granted that you would come.

meaning: To feel that criticism or a comment is directed at you and be hurt by it.
usage: Common advice: “Don't take it personally.”
examples: Don't take it personally; he's rude to everyone.
She takes criticism too personally.
I try not to take bad reviews personally.
He took the rejection personally.

meaning: To try to do something.
usage: British, informal. Pattern: have a go at (doing) something. “Have a go at someone” also means to criticize them.
examples: I've never surfed, but I'd love to have a go.
Have a go at answering the question yourself.
Let me have a go at fixing it.
My boss had a go at me for being late.

meaning: To look at something briefly.
usage: Pattern: have a look at something; have a quick look. American English also “take a look”.
examples: Can I have a look at your notes?
Have a look at this photo.
I'll have a quick look at your essay.
Let's have a look around the market.

meaning: To have a friendly, informal conversation.
usage: Pattern: have a chat with someone about something. British and informal.
examples: Let's have a chat over coffee.
I had a chat with my neighbour this morning.
Can we have a quick chat about the project?
We had a long chat about our plans.

meaning: To speak briefly to someone, often privately or about a problem.
usage: Common phrase: “Can I have a word with you?” It can signal a serious talk.
examples: Can I have a word with you in private?
I'll have a word with the manager about the noise.
You should have a word with him about his behaviour.
The teacher wants to have a word with your parents.

meaning: To start to doubt a decision you have made.
usage: Pattern: have second thoughts about (doing) something. Also: on second thoughts (British) / on second thought (American).
examples: I'm having second thoughts about moving abroad.
She had second thoughts and cancelled the order.
If you have second thoughts, let me know.
He never had second thoughts about his career choice.

meaning: To like eating sweet food very much.
usage: Informal and common. Always singular “tooth”.
examples: I have a real sweet tooth; I can't resist chocolate.
My grandfather has a sweet tooth.
If you have a sweet tooth, try this dessert.
Children often have a sweet tooth.

meaning: To disagree angrily with someone.
usage: Pattern: have an argument with someone about/over something. Also: get into an argument.
examples: I had an argument with my brother about money.
They had a big argument over where to go on holiday.
We never have arguments about housework.
She had an argument with the taxi driver.

meaning: To have a good or valid idea or argument.
usage: Common response: “You have a point” (I partly agree). Also: “She's got a point.”
examples: You have a point; maybe we should wait.
I hate to admit it, but he has a point.
She has a point about the cost.
Critics have a point when they say the plan is too expensive.

meaning: To learn how to do something, especially after practice.
usage: Informal. Pattern: get the hang of (doing) something.
examples: Driving is hard at first, but you'll get the hang of it.
I'm finally getting the hang of using chopsticks.
It took me a week to get the hang of the new software.
Once you get the hang of it, it's easy.

meaning: To remove or throw away something unwanted.
usage: Common in everyday speech: get rid of old clothes/a cold/a habit/a problem.
examples: I need to get rid of some old clothes.
How can I get rid of this headache?
We got rid of the old sofa.
It's hard to get rid of bad habits.

meaning: To contact someone.
usage: Pattern: get in touch with someone. Common in emails: “Please get in touch if you have any questions.”
examples: Please get in touch if you have any questions.
I'll get in touch with you next week.
She got in touch with an old school friend on Facebook.
How can I get in touch with the manager?

meaning: To have a friendly relationship with someone.
usage: British English also “get on with”. Pattern: get along well with someone.
examples: I get along well with my colleagues.
Do you get along with your parents?
The two brothers don't get along.
She's easy to get along with.

meaning: To annoy someone, especially by repeated behaviour.
usage: Informal. Also: really get on my nerves.
examples: His constant whistling gets on my nerves.
That song really gets on my nerves.
Stop it; you're getting on my nerves!
Her complaining started to get on everyone's nerves.

meaning: To talk about the most important thing without wasting time.
usage: Often a request: “Please get to the point.” Also: come to the point.
examples: Please get to the point; we don't have much time.
He talked for ten minutes before getting to the point.
Let me get straight to the point.
Good emails get to the point quickly.

meaning: To control your emotions and behave more calmly or sensibly.
usage: Informal and sometimes rude when said to someone: “Get a grip!” Also: get a grip on something (understand/control it).
examples: Get a grip! It's only a small spider.
I need to get a grip and start studying.
The government must get a grip on inflation.
She told herself to get a grip before the interview.

meaning: To become familiar with something so that it is no longer strange or difficult.
usage: Followed by a noun or -ing: get used to the weather / get used to getting up early. Don't confuse with “used to + verb” (past habit).
examples: I'm still getting used to the cold weather.
You'll soon get used to driving on the left.
It took me months to get used to living alone.
She never got used to the noise of the city.

meaning: To continue to communicate with someone.
usage: Pattern: keep in touch with someone. Also: stay in touch. Opposite: lose touch.
examples: Let's keep in touch after graduation.
I keep in touch with my old classmates online.
It's hard to keep in touch when you live far away.
Keep in touch and let me know how you're doing.

meaning: To watch or look after someone or something carefully.
usage: Informal. Also: keep a close eye on.
examples: Can you keep an eye on my bag for a minute?
Keep an eye on the children while I cook.
Investors are keeping a close eye on interest rates.
Keep an eye on the weather forecast.

meaning: To not tell anyone something you have been asked to keep private.
usage: Opposite: let out/reveal/give away a secret. “Can you keep a secret?”
examples: Can you keep a secret?
She's terrible at keeping secrets.
He kept the secret for twenty years.
It's hard to keep a secret in a small town.

meaning: To stay relaxed and not panic.
usage: Also: stay calm. Famous slogan: “Keep calm and carry on.”
examples: Keep calm and call for help.
It's important to keep calm in an emergency.
She kept calm during the interview.
Try to keep calm, even when people are rude.

meaning: To do what you said you would do.
usage: Opposite: break a promise. Also: keep your word.
examples: He always keeps his promises.
Politicians rarely keep their promises.
I promised to call, and I kept my promise.
Don't make promises you can't keep.

meaning: To stay informed about something or record it so that you know what is happening.
usage: Opposite: lose track of. Typical objects: spending, time, progress, changes.
examples: I use an app to keep track of my spending.
It's hard to keep track of all the new rules.
Keep track of your progress in a notebook.
Teachers keep track of students' attendance.

meaning: To move or progress at the same speed as someone or something; to stay informed.
usage: Typical objects: the news, technology, demand, classmates, the latest trends.
examples: It's hard to keep up with all the new technology.
She walks so fast that I can't keep up with her.
I read the news to keep up with current events.
The factory can't keep up with demand.

meaning: To stay healthy and strong through exercise.
usage: British English. Also: stay fit/in shape. A “keep-fit class” is an exercise class.
examples: I go swimming to keep fit.
My grandmother keeps fit by walking every day.
Keeping fit helps reduce stress.
He joined a gym to keep fit.

meaning: To fail to do what you promised.
usage: Opposite: keep a promise. Irregular: broke, broken.
examples: He broke his promise to call me.
Never break a promise to a child.
The government broke its promise not to raise taxes.
I'm sorry I broke my promise.

meaning: To tell someone about something important, especially bad news.
usage: Pattern: break the news to someone. Often: break the news gently.
examples: The doctor broke the news to the family.
How should I break the news to my parents?
She broke the news that she was leaving.
He broke the news gently.

meaning: To do or say something to make people feel more relaxed, especially when they first meet.
usage: Related noun: an icebreaker (an activity or comment to help people relax).
examples: He told a joke to break the ice.
Games are a good way to break the ice in class.
It was awkward at first, but she soon broke the ice.
A compliment can help break the ice.

meaning: To stop doing something you do regularly, especially something bad.
usage: Also: kick a habit (informal). Opposite: form/develop a habit.
examples: It's hard to break a habit like smoking.
I'm trying to break the habit of checking my phone in bed.
It takes weeks to break a bad habit.
She finally broke the habit of biting her nails.

meaning: To do something better, faster, or more than anyone before.
usage: Also: set a record; a world/all-time record; record-breaking.
examples: She broke the world record for the 100 metres.
Temperatures broke records across Europe this summer.
The film broke box office records.
He's trying to break the record for the longest swim.

meaning: To do something that is not allowed.
usage: Opposite: follow/obey the rules. Also: break the law.
examples: Students who break the rules will be punished.
He was sent off for breaking the rules.
Sometimes you have to break the rules to be creative.
She never breaks the rules.

meaning: To become ill with a cold.
usage: Irregular: caught. Also: catch the flu/a virus; have a cold.
examples: Wear a coat or you'll catch a cold.
I caught a cold on the plane.
Children catch colds easily at school.
She caught a bad cold last week.

meaning: To get on a bus in time, or to travel by bus.
usage: Also: catch a train/plane/flight. Opposite: miss the bus.
examples: I catch the bus to work every morning.
We ran to catch the bus.
If you hurry, you'll catch the last bus.
She caught the bus into town.

meaning: To attract someone's attention.
usage: Two uses: something catches your eye (you notice it); you catch someone's eye (you get them to look at you).
examples: A red dress in the window caught my eye.
I tried to catch the waiter's eye.
The headline caught everyone's eye.
She caught my eye across the room and smiled.

meaning: To sleep more than usual to make up for not sleeping enough before.
usage: Also: catch up on work/news/a TV series.
examples: I'm going to catch up on sleep this weekend.
After the exams, she finally caught up on sleep.
You can't really catch up on sleep in one night.
New parents rarely get to catch up on sleep.

meaning: To go and see a person or place.
usage: Pattern: pay someone a visit; pay a visit to somewhere. Irregular: paid.
examples: We paid a visit to my grandparents at the weekend.
You should pay a visit to the museum while you're here.
The president paid a visit to the flood area.
I'll pay you a visit next time I'm in town.

meaning: To say something nice about someone.
usage: Pattern: pay someone a compliment. Also: give a compliment; receive a compliment.
examples: He paid me a compliment on my cooking.
She's good at paying compliments.
It's nice to pay someone a compliment.
I was surprised when the manager paid me a compliment.

meaning: To suffer the bad results of something you have done.
usage: Pattern: pay the price for something. Also: pay a heavy/high price.
examples: If you don't study now, you'll pay the price later.
He paid the price for driving too fast.
The environment is paying the price for our consumption.
Many workers paid a heavy price for the company's mistakes.

meaning: To use less time to do something.
usage: Also: save money/energy/space. Adjective: time-saving.
examples: Online shopping saves a lot of time.
Let's take a taxi to save time.
Planning your week can save time.
This app helps students save time on homework.

meaning: To use time badly or on something pointless.
usage: Patterns: waste time (on) doing something; a waste of time.
examples: Don't waste time worrying about things you can't change.
I wasted so much time on social media this afternoon.
Stop wasting time and get to work.
We wasted time arguing instead of solving the problem.

meaning: To do something unimportant while waiting.
usage: Pattern: kill time (by) doing something. Informal.
examples: I killed time at the airport by reading.
We played cards to kill time.
He browsed the shops to kill time before the film.
Waiting rooms are full of people trying to kill time.

meaning: To have no time left to finish something.
usage: Also: run out of money/patience/ideas. Irregular: ran.
examples: I ran out of time and couldn't finish the exam.
We're running out of time to make a decision.
Hurry up, we're running out of time!
She ran out of time before answering the last question.

meaning: To use time doing something or being with someone.
usage: Patterns: spend time (on) doing something; spend time with someone. Irregular: spent.
examples: I love spending time with my family.
She spends a lot of time reading.
How much time do you spend on your phone?
We spent time exploring the old town.

meaning: Time spent giving full attention to someone you care about.
usage: Uncountable. Pattern: spend quality time with someone.
examples: Busy parents try to spend quality time with their children.
We need more quality time together.
Turn off your phone and enjoy some quality time.
Weekends are our quality time as a family.

meaning: To make short trips to do small tasks, such as shopping or going to the post office.
usage: Pattern: run errands for someone. Informal and common.
examples: I spent the morning running errands.
She runs errands for her elderly neighbour.
I need to run a few errands before dinner.
He ran errands all afternoon.

meaning: To be later than planned.
usage: Common in messages: “Sorry, I'm running late.” Also: run behind schedule.
examples: Sorry, I'm running late; I'll be there in ten minutes.
The train is running late.
The meeting ran late, so I missed dinner.
If you're running late, please text me.

meaning: To fill a bathtub with water.
usage: Pattern: run someone a bath. “Run” here means let water flow.
examples: I ran a hot bath after a long day.
Could you run the kids a bath?
She ran a bath and lit some candles.
Don't forget to turn off the tap when you run a bath.

meaning: To decide something after thinking or discussing.
usage: Also: make/reach a decision. Irregular: came.
examples: We've finally come to a decision.
It took them weeks to come to a decision.
Have you come to a decision about the job?
The jury came to a decision after two days.

meaning: To finish.
usage: Also: draw to a close; bring something to an end.
examples: All good things must come to an end.
The holiday came to an end too quickly.
The war finally came to an end in 1945.
The concert came to an end with fireworks.

meaning: To happen in the way someone hoped or predicted.
usage: Typical subjects: a dream, a wish, a prediction.
examples: Visiting Japan was a dream come true.
I hope your wishes come true.
His prediction came true.
Her dream of becoming a doctor finally came true.

meaning: To be unexpected.
usage: Pattern: come as a surprise to someone; come as no surprise (be expected).
examples: The news came as a surprise to everyone.
It came as no surprise that he won.
Her resignation came as a complete surprise.
The result shouldn't come as a surprise.

meaning: To be useful at some time.
usage: Informal. Often about things you keep just in case.
examples: Keep this bag; it might come in handy.
My Spanish came in handy in Mexico.
A torch will come in handy if the power goes out.
Those extra chairs came in handy at the party.

meaning: To be unable to pay your debts and have to stop trading.
usage: Also: go out of business; declare bankruptcy. Irregular: went, gone.
examples: The company went bankrupt after the recession.
Many restaurants went bankrupt during the pandemic.
If sales don't improve, we'll go bankrupt.
He went bankrupt twice before succeeding.

meaning: To spread very quickly and widely on the internet.
usage: Typical subjects: a video, post, photo, tweet.
examples: Her video went viral overnight.
The post went viral and was shared millions of times.
Companies hope their adverts will go viral.
A photo of the cat went viral on social media.

meaning: To stop trading because of failure.
usage: Also: close down; go bankrupt; go bust (informal).
examples: The bookshop went out of business last year.
Many small firms have gone out of business.
Without customers, we'll go out of business.
The factory went out of business after fifty years.

meaning: To walk somewhere for pleasure or exercise.
usage: Also: take a walk; go for a run/swim/drive.
examples: Let's go for a walk after dinner.
I go for a walk every morning.
We went for a walk along the beach.
Going for a walk helps me think.

meaning: To travel somewhere for a holiday.
usage: British English; American English: go on vacation. Also: be on holiday.
examples: We're going on holiday to Thailand.
Where did you go on holiday last year?
They go on holiday every summer.
I can't wait to go on holiday.

meaning: To say what is true.
usage: Avoid “say the truth”. Common phrase: to tell (you) the truth (= honestly).
examples: Always tell the truth.
To tell the truth, I didn't enjoy the film.
I don't think he's telling the truth.
She finally told the truth about what happened.

meaning: To say something that is not true.
usage: Avoid “say a lie”. Also: tell lies; a white lie (a harmless lie).
examples: Never tell a lie to your doctor.
He told a lie to avoid getting into trouble.
Children sometimes tell lies.
I told a white lie about liking the gift.

meaning: To recognize how two things are different.
usage: Pattern: tell the difference between A and B. Often with “can't”.
examples: I can't tell the difference between the twins.
Can you tell the difference between real and fake leather?
Most people can't tell the difference.
It's hard to tell the difference between the two wines.

meaning: To say something funny to make people laugh.
usage: Avoid “say a joke”. Also: crack a joke (informal).
examples: My grandfather loves telling jokes at family dinners.
She's great at telling jokes.
Can you tell a joke in English?
My dad tells the same jokes every year.

meaning: To become thinner.
usage: Opposite: put on/gain weight. Irregular: lost.
examples: I've lost weight since I started cycling.
She's trying to lose weight before the wedding.
Losing weight takes time and patience.
He lost a lot of weight after changing his diet.

meaning: To become heavier.
usage: Also: gain weight. Opposite: lose weight. Irregular: put, put, put.
examples: I put on weight over the holidays.
He's put on a bit of weight since he stopped running.
Some medicines make you put on weight.
Eating late at night can cause you to put on weight.

meaning: To suddenly become very angry.
usage: Pattern: lose your temper with someone. Opposite: keep your temper. Irregular: lost.
examples: I lost my temper and shouted at him.
She rarely loses her temper.
Try not to lose your temper with the children.
He lost his temper when the computer crashed again.

meaning: To not notice how much time has passed.
usage: Also: lose track of something/someone (stop knowing where it is or what is happening).
examples: I was so engrossed in the book that I lost track of time.
Sorry I'm late; I lost track of time.
It's easy to lose track of time on social media.
We were chatting and completely lost track of time.

meaning: To stop communicating with someone over time.
usage: Pattern: lose touch with someone. Also: lose touch with reality (no longer understand the real situation).
examples: I lost touch with most of my school friends.
We lost touch after she moved abroad.
Don't lose touch; send me a message sometimes.
Some politicians have lost touch with ordinary people.

meaning: To worry a lot about something.
usage: Often negative: “Don't lose sleep over it” (don't worry).
examples: Don't lose sleep over one bad grade.
I'm not going to lose sleep over what he said.
She lost sleep over the decision for weeks.
It's not worth losing sleep over.

meaning: To become heavier.
usage: Also: put on weight. Opposite: lose weight.
examples: Many people gain weight in winter.
She gained weight after she stopped exercising.
Stress can cause you to gain weight.
The baby is gaining weight steadily.

meaning: To get knowledge or skill by doing something.
usage: Also: get/acquire experience; valuable/practical/work experience.
examples: Internships help students gain experience.
I volunteered to gain experience in teaching.
She gained a lot of experience working abroad.
It's hard to get a job without experience, and hard to gain experience without a job.

meaning: A large number of vehicles on the road.
usage: Avoid “big traffic”. Also: light traffic; get stuck in heavy traffic.
examples: We got stuck in heavy traffic on the way home.
There's always heavy traffic in the city centre at 5 p.m.
Allow extra time because of heavy traffic.
Heavy traffic delayed the ambulance.

meaning: A large amount of rain.
usage: Avoid “strong rain”. Also: heavy snow; light rain.
examples: Heavy rain caused flooding in the city.
The match was cancelled because of heavy rain.
Heavy rain is forecast for tomorrow.
We walked home in heavy rain.

meaning: A person who smokes a lot of cigarettes.
usage: Also: a heavy drinker. Opposite: a light/occasional smoker.
examples: My grandfather was a heavy smoker.
Heavy smokers are at greater risk of lung disease.
She used to be a heavy smoker but quit last year.
He's a heavy smoker and coughs all the time.

meaning: A way of speaking that clearly shows where someone comes from.
usage: Also: a heavy/thick accent; a slight accent. Pattern: speak with a strong accent.
examples: He speaks English with a strong French accent.
Her strong accent was hard to understand at first.
Having a strong accent is nothing to be ashamed of.
The actor put on a strong Scottish accent.

meaning: Coffee with a lot of flavour and caffeine.
usage: Avoid “heavy coffee”. Also: strong tea; weak coffee.
examples: I need a cup of strong coffee to wake up.
Vietnamese coffee is famously strong.
Strong coffee keeps me awake at night.
She likes her coffee strong and black.

meaning: A small meal that does not make you feel full.
usage: Opposite: a heavy/big meal. Also: a light lunch/snack.
examples: I had a light meal before the concert.
The café serves light meals and snacks.
Eat a light meal before exercising.
We just want a light meal tonight.

meaning: A situation in which you only just avoid danger or disaster.
usage: Verbs: have a narrow escape. Similar: a close call, a near miss.
examples: We had a narrow escape when a tree fell near our car.
The climbers had a narrow escape in the storm.
It was a narrow escape; the bus almost hit him.
She had a narrow escape from the fire.

meaning: A friend you know very well and like very much.
usage: Also: a close relative/relationship; close friends with someone.
examples: She's one of my closest friends.
I told only a close friend about my plans.
A close friend helped me through a difficult time.
We've been close friends since school.

meaning: A situation where something bad almost happened.
usage: Informal. Similar: a narrow escape, a near miss. Also: a close decision.
examples: That was a close call; we nearly missed the flight.
The car almost hit me; it was a close call.
The election was a close call.
After that close call, he drives more carefully.

meaning: A very painful feeling of disappointment.
usage: Also: a great/huge disappointment. “Bitter” also collocates with cold, wind, experience, end.
examples: Losing the final was a bitter disappointment.
Not getting into university was a bitter disappointment for her.
The cancellation came as a bitter disappointment to fans.
He hid his bitter disappointment well.

meaning: A very small possibility.
usage: Also: a small/slight/remote chance. Opposite: a good/high chance.
examples: There's only a slim chance of finding survivors.
We have a slim chance of winning.
There's a slim chance the shop is still open.
Even with a slim chance, it's worth trying.

meaning: Used sarcastically to mean no chance at all.
usage: Very informal, usually as an exclamation: “Fat chance!” Note: despite “fat”, it means the opposite of a big chance.
examples: “Do you think he'll lend you his car?” “Fat chance!”
Fat chance of getting a table on a Saturday night.
A pay rise this year? Fat chance.
There's a fat chance of him apologizing.

meaning: A serious error.
usage: Also: a huge/terrible/costly mistake. Verb: make a big mistake.
examples: Leaving my job was a big mistake.
You're making a big mistake.
Admitting a big mistake takes courage.
Ignoring the problem would be a big mistake.

meaning: An error that many people make.
usage: Pattern: a common mistake is to… / A common mistake among learners is…
examples: A common mistake is to say “I am agree”.
Forgetting to save your work is a common mistake.
This is a common mistake among beginners.
The teacher explained some common mistakes in essays.

meaning: A general, approximate idea.
usage: Pattern: have/give someone a rough idea of something. Also: a rough estimate/guess.
examples: Can you give me a rough idea of the cost?
I have a rough idea of what I want to say.
We only have a rough idea of the timeline.
Give me a rough idea of how long it will take.

meaning: An unclear or uncertain idea.
usage: Also: not have the vaguest idea (not know at all). Similar: a faint/hazy idea.
examples: I have a vague idea of where the station is.
She had only a vague idea of what the job involved.
I haven't the vaguest idea what you mean.
He had a vague idea of becoming a writer.

meaning: Pain in the throat, often from a cold.
usage: Also: have/get a sore throat. Other collocations with “sore”: sore eyes/muscles/feet.
examples: I've got a sore throat and a headache.
Drink honey and lemon for a sore throat.
Singing all night gave me a sore throat.
A sore throat is often the first sign of a cold.

meaning: A very bad headache.
usage: Informal. Also: a terrible/pounding headache.
examples: I woke up with a splitting headache.
The noise gave me a splitting headache.
She went home with a splitting headache.
A splitting headache kept me awake all night.

meaning: A nose that has liquid coming out of it, usually because of a cold.
usage: Also: a blocked/stuffy nose. Common symptom descriptions with a doctor.
examples: The baby has a runny nose and a cough.
I've had a runny nose all week.
Allergies can cause a runny nose.
Bring tissues if you have a runny nose.

meaning: A cold with strong symptoms.
usage: Also: a heavy/nasty cold. Verbs: have/catch/get over a bad cold.
examples: I've got a bad cold, so I'm staying home.
She's getting over a bad cold.
A bad cold kept him off work for a week.
I caught a bad cold on holiday.

meaning: A quick return to good health.
usage: Common phrase in cards and messages: “Wishing you a speedy recovery.” Also: a full/quick recovery.
examples: We wish you a speedy recovery.
Thanks to good care, she made a speedy recovery.
Rest is the key to a speedy recovery.
Everyone hopes the player makes a speedy recovery.

meaning: A diet with the right amounts of different kinds of healthy food.
usage: Verbs: eat/have/follow/maintain a balanced diet. Also: a healthy diet.
examples: A balanced diet includes plenty of fruit and vegetables.
Children need a balanced diet to grow.
It's hard to eat a balanced diet when you're busy.
Exercise and a balanced diet keep you healthy.

meaning: A way of living that keeps you physically and mentally well.
usage: Verbs: lead/live/maintain/promote a healthy lifestyle. Opposite: an unhealthy lifestyle.
examples: Leading a healthy lifestyle reduces the risk of disease.
Schools should promote a healthy lifestyle.
A healthy lifestyle includes enough sleep.
She changed her habits to live a healthy lifestyle.

meaning: A way of living that involves a lot of sitting and little exercise.
usage: Verbs: lead/have a sedentary lifestyle. Common in health articles.
examples: A sedentary lifestyle increases the risk of heart disease.
Many office workers lead a sedentary lifestyle.
Children today have a more sedentary lifestyle.
Short walks can counter the effects of a sedentary lifestyle.

meaning: Sleeping deeply.
usage: Used after “be”: be fast asleep. Also: sound asleep. “Fast” here means firmly.
examples: The children are fast asleep.
By ten o'clock, he was fast asleep.
She was fast asleep when the phone rang.
I fell fast asleep on the train.

meaning: Completely awake.
usage: Used after verbs like be/lie/stay. Opposite: fast asleep.
examples: I was wide awake at 3 a.m.
The coffee kept me wide awake all night.
She lay wide awake, worrying about the exam.
The baby is wide awake and wants to play.

meaning: Extremely cold, in an unpleasant way.
usage: Also: a bitterly cold wind/morning. “Bitterly” also collocates with disappointed, regret, complain.
examples: It was bitterly cold outside this morning.
A bitterly cold wind blew across the square.
We waited for the bus in bitterly cold weather.
Winters here are bitterly cold.

meaning: Extremely hot.
usage: Informal intensifier. Also: freezing cold; scorching hot.
examples: It's boiling hot in here; can we open a window?
The soup is boiling hot, so be careful.
We spent a boiling hot day at the beach.
Summers in Hanoi are boiling hot.

meaning: Completely wet.
usage: Informal. Also: wet through; drenched; soaked.
examples: I got soaking wet walking home in the rain.
Take off those soaking wet clothes.
The dog came in soaking wet.
My shoes are still soaking wet.

meaning: Completely dark.
usage: Also: pitch black. Often with “it was”: “It was pitch dark.”
examples: It was pitch dark when we got home.
The room was pitch dark after the power cut.
We walked through the pitch dark forest.
I couldn't see anything; it was pitch dark.

meaning: Completely new and never used before.
