usage: Hyphenated before a noun in some styles (brand-new). Also: a brand new car/phone/start.
examples: She bought a brand new car.
The phone is brand new; I haven't used it yet.
Moving abroad felt like a brand new start.
The school has a brand new library.

meaning: Very clear and easy to see through; also, very easy to understand.
usage: Common phrase: “Let me make this crystal clear.” Also: crystal clear water.
examples: The water was crystal clear.
Let me make this crystal clear: no phones in class.
Her instructions were crystal clear.
It's crystal clear that he's not interested.

meaning: Very sorry.
usage: Formal and sincere. Also: deeply regret/grateful/concerned.
examples: I'm deeply sorry for your loss.
We are deeply sorry for the inconvenience.
He said he was deeply sorry for his mistake.
I'm deeply sorry if I offended you.

meaning: Strongly advised as good.
usage: Also: highly regarded/skilled/qualified/likely. Common in reviews.
examples: This restaurant comes highly recommended.
The book is highly recommended for beginners.
Booking in advance is highly recommended.
Her course was highly recommended by former students.

meaning: Completely conscious of something.
usage: Patterns: fully aware of something/that… Also: well aware.
examples: I'm fully aware of the risks.
She was fully aware that she was late.
Make sure staff are fully aware of the new rules.
We are fully aware of the problem and are working on it.

meaning: Completely foolish or unreasonable.
usage: “Utterly” intensifies negative or extreme adjectives: utterly exhausted/useless/wrong.
examples: That's an utterly ridiculous idea.
The price was utterly ridiculous.
It's utterly ridiculous to wait three hours for a train.
His excuse was utterly ridiculous.

meaning: Extremely pleased.
usage: “Absolutely” goes with extreme adjectives: absolutely amazing/exhausted/furious. Avoid “very delighted”.
examples: We're absolutely delighted with the result.
She was absolutely delighted to win.
I'd be absolutely delighted to come.
The parents were absolutely delighted with the school.

meaning: Completely normal; nothing to worry about.
usage: Also: perfectly fine/natural/reasonable. Often reassuring: “It's perfectly normal to feel nervous.”
examples: It's perfectly normal to feel nervous before an exam.
The test results are perfectly normal.
Making mistakes is perfectly normal when learning.
It's perfectly normal for babies to cry at night.

meaning: Very sick, in a way that may be dangerous.
usage: Also: seriously injured/damaged. Similar: critically/gravely ill.
examples: Her father is seriously ill in hospital.
He was seriously ill as a child.
Seriously ill patients are treated first.
She became seriously ill after the trip.

meaning: Married and happy in the marriage.
usage: Often in descriptions of people: “They've been happily married for 40 years.”
examples: They've been happily married for thirty years.
She's happily married with two children.
My grandparents were happily married their whole lives.
Despite rumours, the couple are happily married.

meaning: Extremely shy, in a way that causes difficulty.
usage: “Painfully” also collocates with obvious, slow, aware, thin.
examples: As a child, she was painfully shy.
He's painfully shy around strangers.
Being painfully shy made school difficult.
The painfully shy boy grew into a confident speaker.

meaning: Totally unlike something else.
usage: Also: totally/entirely/quite different. Pattern: completely different from/to.
examples: The city is completely different from what I expected.
My brother and I are completely different.
She looks completely different with short hair.
That's a completely different issue.

meaning: Completely not acceptable.
usage: Also: completely/absolutely unacceptable. Used to express strong disapproval.
examples: This kind of behaviour is totally unacceptable.
Waiting two hours is totally unacceptable.
Racist comments are totally unacceptable.
The service was totally unacceptable.

meaning: To disagree very much.
usage: Also: strongly agree/believe/recommend/oppose. Common in surveys and essays.
examples: I strongly disagree with this decision.
Many teachers strongly disagree with the new policy.
She strongly disagreed but said nothing.
Do you agree or strongly disagree with the statement?

meaning: To remember something only a little.
usage: Opposite: clearly/vividly remember. Also: vaguely familiar.
examples: I vaguely remember meeting her at a party.
He vaguely remembers his first day at school.
I only vaguely remember the film.
She vaguely remembered his face.

meaning: To say sorry in a truly meant way.
usage: Formal. British spelling also “apologise”. Common in official apologies: “We sincerely apologize for…”.
examples: We sincerely apologize for the delay.
I sincerely apologize for my behaviour.
The company sincerely apologized to its customers.
He sincerely apologized and promised it wouldn't happen again.

meaning: To remember something in detail.
usage: Also: vividly/distinctly remember. Opposite: vaguely remember.
examples: I clearly remember the day we met.
She clearly remembers locking the door.
Do you clearly remember what he said?
I clearly remember my grandmother's kitchen.

meaning: Seriously harmed or broken.
usage: Also: badly hurt/injured/affected. “Badly” intensifies negative states.
examples: The car was badly damaged in the accident.
Many homes were badly damaged by the storm.
His reputation was badly damaged by the scandal.
The old painting is badly damaged.

meaning: The ability to understand and enjoy funny things.
usage: American spelling: humor. Adjectives: a good/great/dry/dark sense of humour.
examples: She has a great sense of humour.
A sense of humour helps in difficult times.
He has a dry sense of humour.
I'm looking for a partner with a good sense of humour.

meaning: The ability to know which way to go; also, a clear idea of your aims in life.
usage: Literal: a good/bad sense of direction. Figurative: lack a sense of direction.
examples: I have a terrible sense of direction and always get lost.
She has a good sense of direction.
After university, he lacked a sense of direction.
The new manager gave the team a sense of direction.

meaning: A feeling of satisfaction after succeeding at something difficult.
usage: Verbs: give/feel/get a sense of achievement. Also: a sense of accomplishment.
examples: Finishing the marathon gave me a real sense of achievement.
Learning a new skill brings a sense of achievement.
She felt a great sense of achievement after graduating.
Small goals give students a sense of achievement.

meaning: A feeling of being accepted and part of a group or place.
usage: Verbs: create/give/feel a sense of belonging. Common in education and community discussions.
examples: Clubs give students a sense of belonging.
Immigrants may struggle to feel a sense of belonging.
A sense of belonging is important for wellbeing.
The company tries to create a sense of belonging among staff.

meaning: A calm situation without noise or disturbance.
usage: Fixed order. Common phrase: “I just want some peace and quiet.”
examples: I just want some peace and quiet.
We moved to the countryside for peace and quiet.
The library offers peace and quiet for studying.
Enjoy the peace and quiet while the kids are asleep.

meaning: Safe and not harmed.
usage: Fixed order. Often used about someone arriving after a journey or danger.
examples: The children arrived home safe and sound.
We're glad you're back safe and sound.
The missing hiker was found safe and sound.
Text me when you get home safe and sound.

meaning: Very annoyed and bored with something that has happened too often.
usage: Pattern: sick and tired of (doing) something. Informal.
examples: I'm sick and tired of your excuses.
She's sick and tired of working weekends.
People are sick and tired of rising prices.
I'm sick and tired of hearing the same complaints.

meaning: Various small items or tasks of little importance.
usage: Fixed order, informal. Similar: bits and pieces.
examples: The drawer is full of odds and ends.
I have a few odds and ends to finish before I leave.
She sold some odds and ends at the market.
We packed the odds and ends into a box.

meaning: The advantages and disadvantages of something.
usage: Fixed order. Verbs: weigh (up)/consider/discuss the pros and cons.
examples: Let's weigh up the pros and cons before deciding.
There are pros and cons to working from home.
The article discusses the pros and cons of nuclear power.
Make a list of the pros and cons.

meaning: The mixture of good and bad experiences in life or a relationship.
usage: Fixed order. Common: every relationship has its ups and downs.
examples: Every marriage has its ups and downs.
The company has had its ups and downs.
Life is full of ups and downs.
We've been through many ups and downs together.

meaning: Official rules that control how something is done.
usage: Fixed order. Often slightly negative, suggesting too many rules: “so many rules and regulations”.
examples: There are too many rules and regulations for small businesses.
Students must follow the school's rules and regulations.
The rules and regulations are explained in the handbook.
Health and safety rules and regulations keep workers safe.

meaning: Various small things or parts.
usage: Fixed order, informal. Similar: odds and ends.
examples: I need to pick up a few bits and pieces from the shop.
The desk was covered in bits and pieces.
I've learned bits and pieces of Japanese.
She packed her bits and pieces into a small bag.

meaning: Generally; on the whole.
usage: Fixed phrase, usually at the start of a sentence. Similar: on the whole, in general.
examples: By and large, the trip was a success.
The students, by and large, did well in the exam.
By and large, people here are very friendly.
The reviews have been positive by and large.

meaning: More than anything else; most importantly.
usage: Fixed order. Used to introduce the most important point.
examples: First and foremost, I'd like to thank my family.
She is first and foremost a teacher.
First and foremost, we need to agree on a budget.
The job is first and foremost about helping people.

meaning: At some time in the future, even if you don't know exactly when.
usage: Fixed order. It suggests something is inevitable.
examples: Sooner or later, you'll have to tell him the truth.
Prices will fall sooner or later.
Everyone makes mistakes sooner or later.
Sooner or later, the secret will come out.

meaning: A single suggestion about what someone should do.
usage: “Advice” is uncountable, so say “a piece of advice”, not “an advice”.
examples: Can I give you a piece of advice?
The best piece of advice I ever received was to be patient.
He gave me a useful piece of advice about interviews.
Here's a piece of advice: always back up your files.

meaning: Something lucky that happens unexpectedly.
usage: Also: a stroke of genius (a brilliant idea).
examples: By a stroke of luck, we found a parking space right outside.
Meeting her was a real stroke of luck.
It was a stroke of luck that the shop was still open.
A stroke of luck saved the company from bankruptcy.

meaning: A sudden, short period of strong anger.
usage: Also: a fit of rage/jealousy/laughter/coughing. Pattern: in a fit of anger.
examples: In a fit of anger, he threw his phone across the room.
She said things in a fit of anger that she later regretted.
He resigned in a fit of anger.
Don't make decisions in a fit of anger.

meaning: A sudden good idea.
usage: Also: a moment/stroke of inspiration; a flash of insight.
examples: The idea for the book came to her in a flash of inspiration.
I had a flash of inspiration in the shower.
A flash of inspiration solved the problem.
Waiting for a flash of inspiration rarely works; start writing.

meaning: A period of clapping to show approval.
usage: Common phrase: “Let's give her a round of applause.” “Applause” is uncountable.
examples: Let's give our speaker a big round of applause.
The performance received a long round of applause.
The audience gave the actors a round of applause.
She got a round of applause for her answer.

meaning: A sudden loud laugh.
usage: Also: a burst of energy/activity/applause/anger.
examples: His joke was met with a burst of laughter.
A burst of laughter came from the next room.
The audience broke into a burst of laughter.
There was a burst of laughter when the teacher fell off his chair.

meaning: A sudden, sharp feeling of guilt.
usage: Also: a pang of jealousy/regret/hunger/sadness. Verb: feel a pang of guilt.
examples: I felt a pang of guilt for not calling my mother.
She ate the last piece of cake with a pang of guilt.
He felt a pang of guilt when he saw her sad face.
A pang of guilt stopped me from lying.

meaning: A sudden strong feeling of longing for the past.
usage: Also: a wave of sadness/relief/panic; a wave of protests (many at once).
examples: Hearing the song brought a wave of nostalgia.
A wave of nostalgia hit me when I visited my old school.
The old photos triggered a wave of nostalgia.
She felt a wave of nostalgia for her childhood.

meaning: To suddenly start crying.
usage: Irregular: burst, burst, burst. Also: burst into laughter/flames/song.
examples: She burst into tears when she heard the news.
The child burst into tears after falling over.
He almost burst into tears during his speech.
I burst into tears of joy when I passed.

meaning: To suddenly start laughing.
usage: Also: burst into laughter. Compare: burst out crying.
examples: We all burst out laughing at his joke.
She burst out laughing when she saw my hat.
I tried to stay serious, but I burst out laughing.
The audience burst out laughing.

meaning: To start sleeping.
usage: Irregular: fell, fallen. Also: go to sleep; drift off.
examples: I fell asleep on the sofa watching TV.
It takes me a long time to fall asleep.
He fell asleep during the lecture.
Reading helps me fall asleep.

meaning: To start to love someone romantically; also, to start to like something very much.
usage: Pattern: fall in love with someone/something.
examples: They fell in love at university.
I fell in love with Vietnam on my first visit.
She fell in love with the house as soon as she saw it.
Have you ever fallen in love?

meaning: To become sick.
usage: Mainly British. Also: become ill; get sick (American).
examples: She fell ill on holiday.
He fell ill with flu last week.
If you fall ill, call the doctor.
Several students fell ill after the trip.

meaning: To break into pieces; also, to fail or stop working effectively; of a person, to become very upset.
usage: Typical subjects: old objects, plans, relationships, people.
examples: My old shoes are falling apart.
Their marriage fell apart after a few years.
The plan fell apart at the last minute.
She fell apart when she heard the news.

meaning: To fail to keep up with others or with a schedule.
usage: Patterns: fall behind with something (work/payments); fall behind in class.
examples: I fell behind with my studies when I was ill.
Don't fall behind with your rent payments.
The project is falling behind schedule.
She fell behind the other runners.

meaning: To become organized or clear, especially after confusion.
usage: Often: everything fell into place.
examples: After months of planning, everything fell into place.
Suddenly the pieces of the mystery fell into place.
Things will fall into place if you're patient.
Once I understood the grammar rule, everything fell into place.

meaning: To feel comfortable and relaxed somewhere.
usage: Also: make yourself at home (polite invitation to relax).
examples: I felt at home in Hanoi right away.
The staff made us feel at home.
It took months to feel at home in the new city.
Do you feel at home in your new job?

meaning: Used to tell someone they are allowed to do something.
usage: Pattern: feel free to do something. Polite and informal: “Feel free to ask questions.”
examples: Feel free to ask if you have any questions.
Please feel free to help yourself to coffee.
Feel free to call me anytime.
You can feel free to leave early.

meaning: To have less money than before and find it hard to pay for things.
usage: Informal. Common in news about the economy.
examples: Families are feeling the pinch as prices rise.
Small businesses are starting to feel the pinch.
We're feeling the pinch since I lost my job.
Students feel the pinch at the end of each month.

meaning: To feel slightly ill.
usage: Informal and polite. Also: be under the weather.
examples: I'm feeling a bit under the weather today.
She stayed home because she felt under the weather.
If you feel under the weather, get some rest.
He's been feeling under the weather all week.

meaning: To feel that you are not included by others.
usage: Also: leave someone out; make someone feel left out.
examples: I felt left out when they spoke in a language I didn't understand.
Invite everyone so nobody feels left out.
The new student felt left out at lunch.
Children feel left out when they're not invited to parties.

meaning: To feel uncomfortable because you are different from the people or situation around you.
usage: Opposite: feel at home.
examples: I felt out of place in my jeans at the formal dinner.
She felt out of place among the older students.
Many immigrants feel out of place at first.
He felt completely out of place at the party.

collocation: feel on top of the world
meaning: To feel extremely happy and successful.
usage: Informal and enthusiastic.
examples: After passing my exams, I felt on top of the world.
She felt on top of the world when she got the job.
Winning the race made him feel on top of the world.
I feel on top of the world today!

meaning: To feel bad because you have done something wrong or not done something.
usage: Pattern: feel guilty about (doing) something. Also: feel bad about.
examples: I feel guilty about not visiting my grandparents.
Don't feel guilty about taking a day off.
She felt guilty about eating the whole cake.
He felt guilty about lying to his friend.

meaning: To make an alarm clock or phone ring at a particular time.
usage: Pattern: set an alarm for 6 a.m. Irregular: set, set, set.
examples: I set an alarm for 6 a.m.
Don't forget to set your alarm.
She sets three alarms so she doesn't oversleep.
I forgot to set the alarm and missed my flight.

meaning: To put plates, knives, forks, and glasses on a table before a meal.
usage: Also: lay the table (British). Opposite: clear the table.
examples: Can you set the table for dinner?
The children help set the table every evening.
She set the table with the best plates.
I'll cook if you set the table.

meaning: To behave in a way that others should copy.
usage: Pattern: set an example to/for someone; set a good/bad example.
examples: Parents should set a good example for their children.
As captain, she sets an example to the team.
Teachers need to set an example.
He set a bad example by arriving late.

meaning: To achieve a result that is the best ever recorded.
usage: Also: break a record; a world/national record. Irregular: set.
examples: She set a new world record in the 200 metres.
The film set a record for ticket sales.
Temperatures set a record this summer.
He set a record that lasted twenty years.

meaning: To enter or visit a place.
usage: Often negative: “I've never set foot in a casino.” Also: set foot on (land, a ship).
examples: I've never set foot in that restaurant.
She vowed never to set foot in the office again.
He was the first person to set foot on the island.
As soon as I set foot in the city, I loved it.

meaning: To want something very much and be determined to get it.
usage: Patterns: set your heart on something/doing something; have your heart set on something.
examples: She set her heart on studying medicine.
He had set his heart on that bike.
Don't set your heart on one university; apply to several.
They set their hearts on buying a house by the sea.

meaning: To bring up children.
usage: Also: raise children; bring up a family (British).
examples: They moved to the countryside to raise a family.
Raising a family in a big city is expensive.
She raised a family while working full-time.
It's a great place to raise a family.

meaning: To speak more loudly, especially because you are angry.
usage: Often negative: “Don't raise your voice at me.”
examples: Please don't raise your voice; I can hear you.
She never raises her voice, even when she's angry.
He raised his voice so everyone at the back could hear.
Teachers shouldn't raise their voices at students.

meaning: To set a limit on what you are willing to accept.
usage: Patterns: draw the line at something; draw a line under something (treat it as finished).
examples: I'll help you move, but I draw the line at carrying the piano.
We need to draw a line between work and private life.
Let's draw a line under the argument and move on.
Where do you draw the line on what is acceptable?

meaning: To open or close curtains.
usage: Context decides whether it means open or close; “draw the curtains back” clearly means open.
examples: She drew the curtains to keep out the sun.
Draw the curtains; it's getting dark.
He drew the curtains back and looked outside.
The curtains were drawn all day.

meaning: To achieve the best that you are capable of.
usage: Also: realize/fulfil your potential.
examples: Good teachers help students reach their full potential.
She never reached her full potential as an athlete.
The programme helps young people reach their full potential.
With hard work, you can reach your full potential.

meaning: To have a possibility of succeeding.
usage: Often negative: not stand a chance. Pattern: stand a chance of (doing) something. Irregular: stood.
examples: Do you think we stand a chance of winning?
Without experience, he doesn't stand a chance.
She stands a good chance of getting the job.
The small team stood no chance against the champions.

meaning: To refuse to change your opinion or position under pressure.
usage: Also: hold your ground. Literally, not moving back in a fight.
examples: She stood her ground and refused to sign.
Stand your ground if you believe you're right.
The workers stood their ground in the negotiations.
He stood his ground despite the criticism.

meaning: To wait in a line of people.
usage: Mainly American English; British English: queue (up).
examples: We stood in line for an hour to buy tickets.
I hate standing in line at the bank.
Fans stood in line overnight for the concert.
Please stand in line and wait your turn.

meaning: To stop breathing for a short time; also, to wait anxiously.
usage: Figurative: “Don't hold your breath” (it probably won't happen soon).
examples: How long can you hold your breath underwater?
We held our breath as the results were announced.
He says he'll fix it, but don't hold your breath.
The whole country held its breath during the final.

meaning: To continue to feel angry with someone for something they did in the past.
usage: Pattern: hold a grudge against someone. Also: bear a grudge.
examples: She still holds a grudge against her old boss.
Don't hold a grudge; life's too short.
He's not the kind of person who holds a grudge.
They held a grudge for years after the argument.

meaning: To wait on the telephone; also, to maintain a position firmly.
usage: Phone use: “Please hold the line.” Figurative: hold the line on prices/policy.
examples: Please hold the line; I'll put you through.
Could you hold the line for a moment?
The government is trying to hold the line on taxes.
The union held the line in negotiations.

meaning: To consider someone to blame for something.
usage: Pattern: hold someone responsible for something. Also: hold someone accountable.
examples: I'll hold you responsible if anything goes wrong.
Parents were held responsible for their children's behaviour.
The company was held responsible for the pollution.
Who should be held responsible for the accident?

meaning: To leave or start a journey.
usage: Informal. Irregular: hit, hit, hit.
examples: It's getting late; let's hit the road.
We hit the road early to avoid traffic.
The band will hit the road for a world tour.
Time to hit the road!

meaning: To go to bed.
usage: Very informal. Also: hit the hay.
examples: I'm exhausted; I'm going to hit the sack.
We hit the sack early before the trip.
He hit the sack after a long day.
Time to hit the sack.

meaning: To like each other immediately.
usage: Informal. Pattern: hit it off (with someone).
examples: We hit it off as soon as we met.
She hit it off with her new colleagues.
I didn't expect them to hit it off.
They hit it off and became best friends.

collocation: hit the nail on the head
meaning: To describe a problem or situation exactly right.
usage: Informal. Often: “You've hit the nail on the head.”
examples: You've hit the nail on the head; that's exactly the problem.
Her comment hit the nail on the head.
He hit the nail on the head when he said we lack leadership.
The report hits the nail on the head.

meaning: To organize a party.
usage: Also: have/give/host a party. Irregular: threw, thrown.
examples: We're throwing a party for her birthday.
They threw a surprise party for their parents.
He threw a huge party when he got the job.
Let's throw a party at the end of term.

meaning: To pretend not to notice something wrong.
usage: Pattern: turn a blind eye to something.
examples: The police turned a blind eye to the illegal parking.
Managers can't turn a blind eye to bullying.
Some teachers turn a blind eye to phones in class.
The government turned a blind eye to corruption.

meaning: To pass a difficult stage and start to improve.
usage: Common in business and health: “The company has turned a corner.”
examples: After months of losses, the company has turned a corner.
The patient seems to have turned a corner.
We're finally turning a corner with the project.
The economy has turned a corner, according to experts.

meaning: To change a situation so that you now have the advantage over someone who had it before.
usage: Pattern: turn the tables on someone.
examples: The team turned the tables and won in the second half.
She turned the tables on her critics.
The underdog turned the tables on the champion.
In the end, the victim turned the tables on the scammer.

meaning: To arrive later than expected.
usage: Informal: “turn up” = arrive/appear. Also: turn up on time/unexpectedly.
examples: He always turns up late to meetings.
Don't turn up late for the interview.
She turned up late and missed the start of the film.
Guests who turn up late may not get a seat.

meaning: To stop working on something for the rest of the day, or to stop completely.
usage: Informal. Also: call it a night.
examples: It's six o'clock; let's call it a day.
After ten years, the band decided to call it a day.
We called it a day after finishing the report.
I'm tired; I'm calling it a day.

meaning: To phone your workplace to say you are ill and cannot come.
usage: Informal and very common.
examples: I had to call in sick this morning.
Half the staff called in sick with flu.
She called in sick for the third time this month.
If you call in sick, tell your manager before 9 a.m.

meaning: If something crosses your mind, you think of it briefly.
usage: Often negative: “It never crossed my mind.”
examples: It never crossed my mind that she might be lying.
Did it cross your mind to call me?
The idea crossed my mind, but I dismissed it.
It crossed my mind that we might be lost.

meaning: To behave in a way that is no longer acceptable.
usage: Also: step over the line. Common when criticizing jokes or behaviour.
examples: His jokes crossed the line.
Criticism is fine, but insults cross the line.
I think you crossed the line there.
The journalist crossed the line by publishing private photos.

meaning: To look like or be similar to someone or something.
usage: Pattern: bear a (striking/close) resemblance to someone. Formal.
examples: She bears a striking resemblance to her grandmother.
The story bears a close resemblance to real events.
The new building bears little resemblance to the original design.
He bears a resemblance to a famous actor.

meaning: To suffer the worst part of something bad.
usage: Pattern: bear the brunt of something (the cuts/the storm/criticism).
examples: Poor families will bear the brunt of the price rises.
Coastal towns bore the brunt of the storm.
Nurses bear the brunt of staff shortages.
She bore the brunt of her boss's anger.

meaning: To accept the bad results of your actions.
usage: Also: suffer/accept the consequences.
examples: If you break the rules, you'll have to face the consequences.
He was ready to face the consequences of his decision.
Companies that pollute should face the consequences.
She refused to face the consequences.

meaning: To accept criticism or punishment for something you have done.
usage: Informal idiom.
examples: It's time to face the music and tell your boss.
He finally had to face the music after the scandal.
Don't run away; face the music.
She faced the music and apologized publicly.

meaning: To do what the directions tell you to do.
usage: Also: follow the rules/advice/recipe/directions. Opposite: ignore the instructions.
examples: Read and follow the instructions carefully.
If you follow the instructions, the furniture is easy to build.
He didn't follow the instructions and broke the machine.
Students must follow the instructions on the exam paper.

meaning: To do the same job or live the same way as someone before you, often a parent.
usage: Common pattern: follow in his/her father's/mother's footsteps.
examples: She followed in her mother's footsteps and became a doctor.
He didn't want to follow in his father's footsteps.
Many actors' children follow in their parents' footsteps.
I hope to follow in my teacher's footsteps.

meaning: To tell someone what you think they should do.
usage: Pattern: give someone advice on/about something. “Advice” is uncountable: “a piece of advice”, not “an advice”.
examples: My teacher gave me some great advice about university.
Can you give me advice on buying a laptop?
Doctors give advice on healthy eating.
I'm not in a position to give advice.

meaning: To help someone.
usage: Pattern: give someone a hand (with something). Informal. Also: lend a hand.
examples: Could you give me a hand with these boxes?
I'll give you a hand with the cooking.
Our neighbours gave us a hand when we moved.
Let me give you a hand.

meaning: To allow other vehicles or people to go first; also, to break or collapse; to be replaced by something.
usage: British road sign: “Give way” (American: yield). Patterns: give way to someone/something.
examples: You must give way to traffic on the right.
The old bridge gave way under the weight.
Her fear gave way to relief.
Cars should give way to pedestrians at crossings.

meaning: To stop believing that something good will happen.
usage: Often negative: “Don't give up hope.” Also: lose hope.
examples: Don't give up hope; you'll find a job soon.
Rescuers refused to give up hope.
She had almost given up hope of seeing him again.
Never give up hope.

meaning: To try doing something to see whether it works or whether you like it.
usage: Informal. Also: give it a go/shot.
examples: I've never surfed, but I'll give it a try.
Give it a try; you might enjoy it.
The recipe looks hard, but let's give it a try.
I was nervous about singing in public, but I decided to give it a try.

collocation: give someone the benefit of the doubt
meaning: To believe someone is telling the truth or acting honestly, even though you are not sure.
usage: Common in disputes and judgements.
examples: I'll give him the benefit of the doubt this time.
The teacher gave her the benefit of the doubt.
We should give new employees the benefit of the doubt.
She gave him the benefit of the doubt and accepted his excuse.

meaning: Used to tell a guest to relax and feel comfortable.
usage: A polite, friendly phrase when welcoming visitors.
examples: Come in and make yourself at home.
Please make yourself at home while I make some tea.
Make yourself at home; the fridge is full.
When you visit us, just make yourself at home.

meaning: To get to know people you have not met before.
usage: Irregular: met. Also: make new friends.
examples: Joining a club is a great way to meet new people.
I love travelling because I meet new people.
It's hard to meet new people when you work from home.
University is a time to meet new people.

meaning: To do your fair share of work in a group.
usage: Often negative: “He's not pulling his weight.”
examples: Everyone in the team needs to pull their weight.
He's not pulling his weight at work.
If you don't pull your weight, others have to do more.
She always pulls her weight with the housework.

meaning: To joke with someone by telling them something untrue.
usage: Informal. Common response: “Are you pulling my leg?”
examples: Are you pulling my leg?
Don't worry, I'm just pulling your leg.
He loves pulling people's legs.
I thought she was pulling my leg, but it was true.

meaning: To take a risk by trying to get more than you already have.
usage: Informal warning: “Don't push your luck.”
examples: You got away with it once; don't push your luck.
He's pushing his luck by asking for another day off.
I won twice, but I won't push my luck.
Don't push your luck with the teacher.

meaning: To decide what to do as things happen, rather than planning in advance.
usage: Informal. Common in plans: “Let's play it by ear.”
examples: We don't have a plan; we'll play it by ear.
Let's play it by ear and see how we feel tomorrow.
I prefer to play it by ear when travelling.
We'll play it by ear depending on the weather.

meaning: To avoid risks.
usage: Informal. Opposite: take a risk.
examples: I'll play it safe and leave early.
Let's play it safe and bring an umbrella.
Investors are playing it safe this year.
She played it safe and chose the easy question.

meaning: To leave very little time to do something.
usage: British, informal. Also: cut it close (American).
examples: You're cutting it fine; the train leaves in five minutes.
We cut it fine but made the flight.
Don't cut it fine on exam day.
Arriving at 8:58 for a 9:00 meeting is cutting it fine.

meaning: To reduce the amount of something you use or spend.
usage: Also: cut down on. Typical objects: spending, sugar, costs.
examples: We're cutting back on eating out to save money.
The company cut back on travel expenses.
Try to cut back on sugar.
Many families are cutting back on spending.

meaning: To eat, drink, or use less of something.
usage: Common with health habits: cut down on coffee/salt/smoking.
examples: The doctor told me to cut down on salt.
I'm trying to cut down on coffee.
Cutting down on screen time improved my sleep.
He cut down on smoking before quitting completely.

meaning: To wait until the next day before making a decision.
usage: Informal advice: “Why don't you sleep on it?”
examples: It's a big decision; sleep on it.
I'll sleep on it and let you know tomorrow.
She slept on it and decided to accept the offer.
Never sign a contract without sleeping on it.

meaning: To go in front of people who have been waiting longer.
usage: British; American: cut in line. Also figurative: jump the queue for treatment.
examples: A man tried to jump the queue at the ticket office.
It's rude to jump the queue.
Paying extra lets you jump the queue.
Some patients pay to jump the queue for surgery.

meaning: To fail to understand the most important part of something.
usage: Often: “You're missing the point.”
examples: You're missing the point; it's not about money.
Critics missed the point of the film.
I think he completely missed the point.
Don't miss the point of the question.

meaning: To lose an opportunity by acting too slowly.
usage: Informal. Also: miss out on something.
examples: If you don't apply now, you'll miss the boat.
Many investors missed the boat on the tech boom.
I waited too long and missed the boat.
Don't miss the boat; tickets are selling fast.

meaning: To seem familiar.
usage: Often: “Does that name ring a bell?” Irregular: rang, rung.
examples: His name rings a bell, but I can't remember him.
Does this song ring a bell?
The address didn't ring a bell.
That story rings a bell; I think I've read it.

meaning: To avoid laughing or smiling when something is funny.
usage: Often with difficulty: “I could hardly keep a straight face.”
examples: I could hardly keep a straight face when he fell.
It's hard to keep a straight face when she tells jokes.
He told the story while keeping a straight face.
Try to keep a straight face during the photo.

meaning: To do something that helps you release strong feelings or energy.
usage: Informal. American English also “blow off steam”.
examples: I go running to let off steam after work.
Kids need time outside to let off steam.
She called her friend to let off steam.
Playing football helps me let off steam.

meaning: To suddenly become nervous about doing something you planned to do.
usage: Informal. Common about weddings and big decisions.
examples: He got cold feet the day before the wedding.
I was going to quit my job, but I got cold feet.
Investors got cold feet and pulled out.
Don't get cold feet now; you've prepared for months.

meaning: Something very easy to do.
usage: Informal. Often: “It was a piece of cake.”
examples: The exam was a piece of cake.
Setting up the new phone was a piece of cake.
Don't worry, it'll be a piece of cake.
For an experienced chef, this dish is a piece of cake.

meaning: Something that seems bad at first but later brings good results.
usage: Common when looking back at difficulties.
examples: Losing that job was a blessing in disguise.
The rain was a blessing in disguise; the museum was empty.
Failing the exam turned out to be a blessing in disguise.
The injury was a blessing in disguise because I discovered painting.

meaning: Very rarely.
usage: Informal. A “blue moon” is a rare second full moon in a month.
examples: I only eat fast food once in a blue moon.
My brother calls once in a blue moon.
We go to the cinema once in a blue moon.
It snows here once in a blue moon.

meaning: The final problem in a series that makes you unable to accept a situation any longer.
usage: From “the straw that broke the camel's back”. Often: “That was the last straw.”
examples: When he forgot my birthday, it was the last straw.
The latest price rise was the last straw for customers.
Being late again was the last straw, so she was fired.
The noise from upstairs was the last straw; we moved out.

meaning: Experiencing stress because of demands or expectations.
usage: Patterns: be/work/feel under pressure; under pressure to do something; perform well under pressure.
examples: I work best under pressure.
Students are under a lot of pressure during exams.
The government is under pressure to cut taxes.
She stayed calm under pressure.

meaning: Suddenly and unexpectedly.
usage: Informal. Common with call, appear, happen.
examples: An old friend called me out of the blue.
The offer came out of the blue.
Out of the blue, she announced she was leaving.
The storm appeared out of the blue.

collocation: on the spur of the moment
meaning: Suddenly, without planning.
usage: Also as an adjective: a spur-of-the-moment decision. Similar: on a whim.
examples: We decided to go to the beach on the spur of the moment.
He bought the car on the spur of the moment.
Nobody planned the party; a few of us decided on the spur of the moment to celebrate.
She quit her job on the spur of the moment.

meaning: With little warning or time to prepare.
usage: British English; American English: on short notice.
examples: The meeting was cancelled at short notice.
Thank you for coming at such short notice.
It's hard to find a babysitter at short notice.
She was asked to give a speech at short notice.

meaning: Deliberately; not by accident.
usage: Opposite: by accident. Also: deliberately, intentionally (more formal).
examples: Did you break it on purpose?
I'm sure he ignored me on purpose.
She arrived early on purpose to get a good seat.
It wasn't an accident; he did it on purpose.

meaning: Without intending to; by chance.
usage: Opposite: on purpose. Also: accidentally.
examples: I deleted the file by accident.
We met by accident at the airport.
Penicillin was discovered by accident.
Sorry, I took your umbrella by accident.

meaning: From memory, perfectly.
usage: Patterns: learn/know something by heart.
examples: I learned the poem by heart.
She knows all the song lyrics by heart.
Actors have to learn their lines by heart.
Do you know your phone number by heart?

meaning: Needing or wanting to do something quickly.
usage: Also: in a rush. Pattern: be in a hurry to do something.
examples: Sorry, I can't talk; I'm in a hurry.
He left in a hurry and forgot his keys.
There's no need to be in a hurry.
She was in a hurry to get home.

meaning: In the period of time between two events.
usage: Also: meanwhile. Often at the start or end of a sentence.
examples: The doctor will see you soon; in the meantime, please fill in this form.
Dinner will be ready at eight. In the meantime, relax.
I'm looking for a job, and in the meantime I'm volunteering.
The repair takes a week, so you can use this phone in the meantime.

meaning: Permanently; forever.
usage: Informal. Common with leave, quit, stop, move.
examples: He left the country for good.
I've quit smoking for good.
Are you moving back for good?
The factory closed for good last year.

meaning: At the latest possible time.
usage: Also as an adjective: a last-minute decision/change/booking.
examples: She always does her homework at the last minute.
The concert was cancelled at the last minute.
We booked the hotel at the last minute.
He changed his mind at the last minute.

meaning: During a journey; also, coming soon.
usage: Patterns: on the way to/home; on my way. Also: a baby on the way (expected).
examples: I'll buy some bread on the way home.
We stopped for lunch on the way to the beach.
Help is on the way.
They have a second baby on the way.

meaning: A plan with many activities and little free time.
usage: Also: a hectic/packed/tight schedule.
examples: Despite her busy schedule, she always makes time for family.
Thank you for fitting me into your busy schedule.
Students often have a busy schedule during exams.
With such a busy schedule, he rarely cooks.

meaning: A very busy week with a lot happening.
usage: Also: a hectic day/schedule/lifestyle.
examples: I've had a hectic week at work.
After a hectic week, I just want to sleep.
Next week will be hectic because of the conference.
It's been a hectic week with three deadlines.

meaning: A tiring day with a lot of work or activity.
usage: Common phrase: “It's been a long day.”
examples: It's been a long day; I'm exhausted.
After a long day at work, I like to cook.
We have a long day ahead of us tomorrow.
Nurses often work long days.

meaning: A relaxed afternoon with little activity.
usage: Also: a lazy Sunday/morning/day.
examples: We spent a lazy afternoon in the park.
There's nothing better than a lazy afternoon with a book.
It was a lazy afternoon by the pool.
Sunday is usually a lazy afternoon at home.

meaning: An evening spent relaxing at home instead of going out.
usage: Informal. Opposite: a night out.
examples: I'm having a quiet night in with a film.
After a busy week, a quiet night in sounds perfect.
We had a quiet night in and ordered pizza.
Sometimes a quiet night in is just what you need.

meaning: An evening spent going out to have fun, for example at a restaurant or bar.
usage: Also: a girls'/boys' night out. Opposite: a night in.
examples: We're planning a night out to celebrate.
I haven't had a night out in months.
A night out in the city can be expensive.
They enjoyed a night out at the theatre.

meaning: A day when you do not have to work.
usage: Patterns: take/have/get a day off. Plural: days off.
examples: I'm taking a day off tomorrow.
What do you do on your day off?
She hasn't had a day off in weeks.
We get two days off a week.

meaning: A day when most people do not work because of an official celebration.
usage: British; American: a national/federal holiday. Also: a bank holiday (UK).
examples: Monday is a public holiday, so the banks are closed.
Tet is the most important public holiday in Vietnam.
Shops may close early on a public holiday.
There are eight public holidays a year in the UK.

meaning: To pay regular costs such as rent, electricity, and phone.
usage: Also figurative: a job that pays the bills (provides enough money). Irregular: paid.
examples: I work two jobs to pay the bills.
It's hard to pay the bills on a low income.
Writing doesn't pay the bills, so she also teaches.
Don't forget to pay the bills before you go away.

meaning: A plan for how much money you will spend each month.
usage: Verbs: make/stick to/plan a monthly budget.
examples: I make a monthly budget to control my spending.
Rent takes up half of my monthly budget.
Sticking to a monthly budget isn't easy.
Apps can help you plan a monthly budget.

meaning: To keep money instead of spending it, or to spend less.
usage: Patterns: save money on something; save money for something.
examples: I'm saving money for a new laptop.
You can save money by cooking at home.
We saved money on flights by booking early.
It's important to save money for emergencies.

meaning: To use money to buy things.
usage: Pattern: spend money on something. Irregular: spent.
examples: I spend too much money on clothes.
She spent all her money on travel.
Don't spend money you don't have.
How much money do you spend on food each week?

meaning: To take money from someone that you will pay back later.
usage: Pattern: borrow money from someone. Compare: lend money to someone (give).
examples: I had to borrow money from my parents.
Many students borrow money to pay for university.
It's risky to borrow money to invest.
Can I borrow some money until Friday?

meaning: To give money to someone that they will pay back later.
usage: Pattern: lend someone money / lend money to someone. Irregular: lent. Opposite direction: borrow.
examples: Could you lend me some money?
Banks lend money to businesses.
I lent him money, and he never paid it back.
Never lend money you can't afford to lose.

meaning: To be very expensive.
usage: Informal. Also: cost an arm and a leg. Irregular: cost, cost, cost.
examples: That car must have cost a fortune.
Eating out in this city costs a fortune.
The repairs cost a fortune.
It doesn't have to cost a fortune to travel.

meaning: To keep some money for a time when you might unexpectedly need it.
usage: Also: put something aside for a rainy day.
examples: My grandmother always told me to save for a rainy day.
We try to save a little for a rainy day every month.
He hadn't saved for a rainy day, so losing his job hit him hard.
It's wise to save for a rainy day, even on a small salary.

meaning: To spend a lot of money on something special.
usage: British, informal. Similar: treat yourself to something.
examples: We splashed out on a fancy dinner for our anniversary.
She splashed out on a new dress.
I don't usually splash out on clothes.
Let's splash out on a nice hotel for once.

meaning: To spend less money because you have less than before.
usage: Informal. Related: belt-tightening (economic cuts).
examples: We'll have to tighten our belts this year.
Rising prices mean many families must tighten their belts.
The government asked people to tighten their belts.
After losing his job, he had to tighten his belt.

meaning: To spend more money than you earn.
usage: Opposite: live within your means.
examples: Many people live beyond their means using credit cards.
If you live beyond your means, you'll end up in debt.
They were living beyond their means for years.
Students who live beyond their means often rely on loans.

meaning: Having enough money to live comfortably; rich.
usage: Also: better off/worse off (in a better/worse situation). Hyphenated before a noun: a well-off family.
examples: Her family is quite well off.
Well-off students can afford to study abroad.
Her grandparents were quite well off, so she never had to worry about tuition fees.
They're not rich, but they're well off.

meaning: Not having enough money.
usage: Informal. Pattern: hard up for money/cash.
examples: I'm a bit hard up this month.
Students are often hard up.
They were very hard up after he lost his job.
If you're hard up, there are free events in the city.

meaning: Something worth the price paid for it.
usage: Patterns: good/great/poor value for money. Common in reviews.
examples: The hotel was great value for money.
Is the expensive phone really value for money?
Customers want value for money.
The set lunch is excellent value for money.
